1.what: This Act may be called the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 and it extends to the whole of India, except the State of Jammu and Kashmir.

2.what: Definitions in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, including explanations and exceptions.

3.what: This section deals with the construction of references to Magistrates, including their jurisdiction and powers, and provides guidelines for interpreting such references in different contexts.

4.what: Offences under Indian Penal Code and other laws shall be investigated, inquired into, tried, and dealt with according to the provisions contained in this section.

5.what: Nothing contained in this Code shall, in the absence of a specific provision to the contrary, affect any special or local law for the time being in force, or any special jurisdiction or power conferred, or any special form of procedure prescribed, by any other law for the time being in force.

6.what: There are four classes of Criminal Courts: Courts of Session, First Class Judicial Magistrates, Second Class Judicial Magistrates, and Executive Magistrates.

7.what: Every State shall be a sessions division or shall consist of sessions divisions; and every sessions divisions shall, for the purposes of this Code, be a district or consist of districts: Provided that every metropolitan area shall, for the said purposes, be a separate sessions division and district.

8.what: A metropolitan area is a city or town with a population over one million. The government can declare an area a metropolitan area by notification. Some cities are already declared as metropolitan areas. The government can change the limits of a metropolitan area, but not if it would reduce the population to less than one million. If an area's population falls below one million, it will no longer be considered a metropolitan area, but any ongoing cases will continue as usual.

9.what: The State Government shall establish a Court of Session for every sessions division, and every Court of Session shall be presided over by a Judge, to be appointed by the High Court.

10.what: Assistant Sessions Judges are subordinate to Sessions Judges and may make rules for distributing business among them.

11.what: There must be at least one Court of Judicial Magistrates of the first class and one of the second class in every district, except metropolitan areas. The High Court appoints presiding officers for these courts. The High Court can give powers to a Judicial Magistrate to act like a judge in a civil court if it thinks it's necessary or expedient.

12.what: The High Court shall appoint a Judicial Magistrate of the first class to be the Chief Judicial Magistrate in every district (not being a metropolitan area), and may appoint any Judicial Magistrate of the first class to be an Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate.

13.what: Special Judicial Magistrates: Powers and Appointment

14.what: Local jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates: The jurisdiction and powers of every Magistrate appointed under sections 11, 13, or 18 extend throughout the district, except where defined by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

15.what: Judicial Magistrates are subordinate to Sessions Judges and Chiefs Judicial Magistrates, with specific rules for distribution of business.

16.what: Courts of Metropolitan Magistrates in metropolitan areas must be established by the State Government with the approval of the High Court, and presiding officers will be appointed by the High Court. The jurisdiction of these courts extends throughout the metropolitan area.

17.what: The High Court appoints a Metropolitan Magistrate to be the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate for a metropolitan area, and may also appoint another Magistrate as an Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate with specified powers.

18.what: The High Court may confer upon any person who holds or has held any post under the Government, all or any of the powers conferred or conferrable by or under this Code on a Metropolitan Magistrate, in respect of particular cases or to particular classes of cases

19.what: The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and every Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate shall be subordinate to the Sessions Judge; and every other Metropolitan Magistrate shall, subject to the general control of the Sessions Judge, be subordinate to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate.

20.what: Executive Magistrates: Appointment, Powers and Responsibilities. The State Government may appoint Executive Magistrates in districts and metropolitan areas. An Executive Magistrate can be appointed as Additional District Magistrate with limited powers. In case of a vacant District Magistrate position, the next officer takes over temporarily until the State Government orders otherwise. The State Government can place an Executive Magistrate in charge of a sub-division and relieve them as needed. The State Government can also delegate its powers to the District Magistrate.

21.what: The State Government may appoint Executive Magistrates with specific powers and functions.

22.what: Executive Magistrates' local jurisdiction: District Magistrates can define areas within which Executive Magistrates have power, but their jurisdiction extends throughout the district unless defined.

23.what: Executive Magistrates are subordinate to: - District Magistrate (except Sub-divisional Magistrates) - Sub-divisional Magistrate (in a sub-division)

24.what: Section 24 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 states that the Government of the Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir may appoint a person who has been in practice as an Advocate for not less than seven years as Public Prosecutor or Additional Public Prosecutor for High Court and for the District Courts.

25.what: The State Government shall appoint in every district one or more Assistant Public Prosecutors for conducting prosecutions in the Courts of Magistrates.

25A.what: Section 25A of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 states that the State Government may establish a Directorate of Prosecution consisting of a Director of Prosecution and as many Deputy Directors of Prosecution as it thinks fit. Additionally, this section empowers the State Government to return all or any part of a case back to the court after it has been referred to the Directorate of Prosecution.

26.what: Offences can be tried by High Court, Court of Session, or specified courts as per the First Schedule.

27.what: Any offence committed by a person under 16 years old may be tried by a Chief Judicial Magistrate or a specially empowered court.

28.what: A High Court, Sessions Judges and Assistant Sessions Judges can pass certain sentences as authorized by law.

29.what: A Magistrate can pass sentences up to: - Imprisonment for more than 7 years (except death) - Fine not exceeding ₹10,000 or both - Imprisonment for more than 1 year (except second-class magistrate) - Fine not exceeding ₹5,000 or both

30.what: The Court of a Magistrate may award a term of imprisonment not exceeding the powers of the Magistrate under section 29, as long as it does not exceed one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment for the offence.

31.what: When a person is convicted of two or more offences at one trial, the Court can sentence them for each offence with punishments that add up to no more than 14 years in prison. The sentences do not have to run consecutively unless the Court decides.

32.what: The High Court or State Government can give official titles to certain persons by order, and these titles take effect from the date of communication.

33.what: Whenever any person holding an office in the service of Government who has been invested with powers under this Code is appointed to an equal or higher office, he shall exercise the same powers in the local area in which he is so appointed

34.what: The High Court or the State Government may withdraw all or any of the powers conferred by it under this Code on any person or by any officer

35.what: The powers and duties of a Judge or Magistrate may be exercised or performed by his successor-in-office.

36.what: Police officers superior in rank to an officer in charge of a police station may exercise the same powers throughout the local area they are appointed to, as the officer within their station's limits.

37.what: Every person must assist a Magistrate or police officer if they reasonably require help, especially when: arresting someone else, preventing a breach of peace, or stopping an attempt to harm public property.

38.what: A person can help execute a warrant given to someone who is not a police officer, as long as that person is nearby and the person receiving the warrant is also helping to carry it out.

39.what: Every person aware of the commission of or intention to commit certain offences punishable under Indian Penal Code sections 121-126, 143-148, 161-165A, 272-278, 302-304, 364A, 382, 392-399, 409, 431-439, 449-450, 456-460, and 489A-489E shall give information to the nearest Magistrate or police officer in the absence of a reasonable excuse.

40.what: Every officer employed in connection with the affairs of a village and every person residing in a village shall forthwith communicate to the nearest Magistrate or to the officer in charge of the nearest police station, whichever is nearer, any information which he may possess respecting certain matters.

41.what: Section 41 states that a police officer may arrest without warrant anyone who commits a cognizable offence in their presence, or against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that they have committed a cognizable offence.

41A.what: complete explanation of Section 41A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973: A police officer must issue a notice to a person who has been accused of committing a cognizable offence, directing them to appear before the officer or at another specified place. The person must comply with the notice's terms. If they do, they cannot be arrested unless the officer believes they should be arrested for reasons recorded.

41B.what: Every police officer while making an arrest shall bear accurate, visible and clear identification of his name, prepare a memorandum of arrest attested by at least one witness and countersigned by the person arrested, and inform the person arrested of their right to have a relative or friend informed of their arrest.

41C.what: The State Government shall establish police control rooms in every district and at the state level. The control room must display the names and addresses of arrested persons and the name and designation of the arresting officers.

41D.what: The arrested person has the right to meet with their chosen advocate during interrogation, but this right does not apply throughout the entire interrogation process.

42.what: When any person who, in the presence of a police officer, has committed or has been accused of committing a non-cognizable offence refuses, on demand, to give his name and residence, he may be arrested by such officer in order that his name or residence may be ascertained.

43.what: A private person can arrest someone who commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence in their presence. The arrested person must be taken to a police station without delay. If the person is believed to have committed an offence under section 41, they will be re-arrested by a police officer. If the person refuses to give their name and residence, or provides false information, they may be dealt with under section 42. Otherwise, they will be released.

44.what: A Magistrate can arrest someone who committed an offence in their presence, or order someone else to do so, and then take them into custody. A Magistrate can also arrest someone without being present if they are competent to issue a warrant at the time and in the circumstances.

45.what: Members of the Armed Forces can only be arrested with Central Government's consent for actions taken in official duties.

46.what: A police officer must physically touch or confine a person during an arrest unless they submit voluntarily.

47.what: A police officer can enter a place where a person to be arrested may be hiding if they have a warrant or are authorized to make an arrest. The officer must give notice and allow the person to leave before entering the apartment of a female who lives there, unless she is the one being arrested. If the officer cannot get into the place, they can break open doors or windows to enter it.

48.what: A police officer may, for the purpose of arresting without warrant any person whom he is authorised to arrest, pursue such person into any place in India.

49.what: The person arrested shall not be subjected to more restraint than is necessary to prevent his escape.

50.what: A police officer must tell a person who is arrested without a warrant: The reasons they were arrested. If the person was not accused of a non-bailable offence, they must also be told: They have the right to be released on bail and can arrange for sureties.

50A.what: Every police officer or other person making any arrest under this Code shall forthwith give the information regarding such arrest and place where the arrested person is being held to any of his friends, relatives or such other persons as may be disclosed or nominated by the arrested person for the purpose of giving such information.

51.what: A person arrested without a warrant or under a warrant that cannot be used for bail can be searched and their belongings taken into custody, except for essential clothing. If an item is seized, the police officer must give the person a receipt.

52.what: The officer can seize any offensive weapon a person has on them during an arrest and must hand it over to the court.

53.what: A registered medical practitioner can examine an arrested person to gather evidence for an offence, with permission from a police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector, and use necessary force.

53A.what: A registered medical practitioner can examine a person accused of rape with force if requested by a police officer, and must report on the examination's details, including the accused's identity, age, injuries, DNA material, and other relevant information.

54.what: When any person is arrested, he shall be examined by a medical officer in the service of Central or State Government, and in case the medical officer is not available, by a registered medical practitioner soon after the arrest is made: Provided that where the arrested person is a female, the examination of the body shall be made only by or under the supervision of a female medical officer, and in case the female medical officer is not available, by a female registered medical practitioner.

54A.what: A court can order a person arrested on suspicion of committing an offence to undergo identification by any person, as decided by the court, with certain exceptions for people who are mentally or physically disabled.

55.what: A police officer can delegate an arrest without a warrant to a subordinate officer, but must provide written instructions stating the person to be arrested and the reason for the arrest. The subordinate officer must notify the person being arrested of the order before making the arrest.

55A.what: The person in custody must provide a safe environment for the arrested person.

56.what: A police officer must take or send an arrested person before a Magistrate or the officer in charge of a police station without delay, except as specified.

57.what: A police officer cannot detain someone arrested without a warrant for more than 24 hours unless there is a special order from a magistrate.

58.what: Officers in charge of police stations must report to the District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate about people arrested without a warrant, regardless of whether they were released on bail or not.

59.what: A person arrested by a police officer cannot be released unless they post their own bond, are granted bail, or receive a special order from a magistrate.

60.what: If a person in lawful custody escapes or is rescued, the person from whose custody he escaped or was rescued may immediately pursue and arrest him in any place in India.

60A.what: No arrest can be made unless it is in accordance with the provisions of this Code or another law that applies.

61.what: Every summons issued by a Court under this Code shall be in writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer or by another officer designated by the High Court.

62.what: A summons must be served by a police officer or a court official, and can also be served by a public servant, following specific rules.

63.what: Service of a summons can be made to a corporation by: 1) Serving it on the secretary, local manager or principal officer, 2) Sending a letter by registered post to the chief officer in India. The service is considered complete when the letter would arrive normally.

65.what: If service of a summons cannot be done by following the usual method, the serving officer must try alternative methods. They can attach the summons to something visible outside the person's home where they usually live. The court will then decide if this is enough or order new service in a different way.

66.what: The court issuing a summons to a government servant must send it to the head of their office in duplicate, who will then serve it and return it to the court.

67.what: When a court sends a summons to someone who lives outside of its own area of authority, it usually sends two copies of the summons to a nearby magistrate.

68.what: When a summons issued by a Court is served outside its local jurisdiction, an affidavit purporting to be made before a Magistrate that such summons has been served, and a duplicate of the summons purporting to be endorsed by the person to whom it was delivered or tendered or with whom it was left, shall be admissible in evidence.

69.what: A Court can direct a copy of a summons to be served by registered post to a witness at their ordinary residence or business place if they cannot be personally served.

70.what: A written warrant of arrest must be: signed by the presiding officer, have the court's seal, and remain in effect until it is cancelled or executed.

71.what: Power to direct security to be taken for a person's attendance before court, specifying number of sureties, amount of bonds, and time of appearance.

72.what: A warrant of arrest can be directed to: 1. One or more police officers. 2. Any other person(s) if immediate execution is necessary and no police officer is available.

73.what: A Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class can direct a warrant for the arrest of certain individuals, including escaped convicts and those accused of non-bailable offences who are evading arrest. The person receiving the warrant must acknowledge it in writing and execute it if the target is on their property. If arrested, they will be handed over to the nearest police officer, who will take them before a Magistrate unless security is provided under section 71.

74.what: A warrant can be executed by any police officer who has the warrant endorsed on them, not just the one it's originally addressed to.

75.what: The police officer or other person executing a warrant of arrest must inform the person being arrested about the contents of the warrant and, if requested, show them the warrant.

76.what: The police officer or other person executing a warrant of arrest shall bring the person arrested before the Court without unnecessary delay, provided that such delay shall not exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate’s Court.

77.what: A warrant of arrest can be executed anywhere in India.

78.what: When a warrant is to be executed outside the local jurisdiction of the Court issuing it, the Court can forward the warrant by post or otherwise to an Executive Magistrate or District Superintendent of Police within the jurisdiction where it is to be executed. The warrant must include the name of the person executing it and, if possible, be executed in the same manner as before.

79.what: A warrant can be executed outside a court's local jurisdiction with the permission of an Executive Magistrate or a police officer of a certain rank, who must endorse their name on the warrant. This endorsement gives them authority to execute the warrant, and they may be assisted by local police if needed.

80.what: A person arrested outside their district must be brought before a specific authority if the issuing court is not nearby.

81.what: The Executive Magistrate or District Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police must direct the removal of an arrested person to the court that issued the warrant, unless the offence is bailable and the person is willing to give bail.

82.what: A court can publish a written proclamation requiring a person to appear at a specified place and time if it believes that person has absconded or is hiding. The proclamation must be publicly read, affixed in conspicuous places, and may also be published in a newspaper. If the proclamation is published correctly, it is conclusive evidence that the requirements have been met.

83.what: The Court issuing a proclamation under section 82 may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, at any time after the issue of the proclamation, order the attachment of any property, movable or immovable, or both, belonging to the proclaimed person: Provided that where at the time of the issue of the proclamation the Court is satisfied, by affidavit or otherwise, that the person in relation to whom the proclamation is to be issued,— (a) is about to dispose of the whole or any part of his property, or (b) is about to remove the whole or any part of his property from the local jurisdiction of the Court, it may order the attachment simultaneously with the issue of the proclamation.

84.what: Claims and objections to attachment of property can be made within 6 months from the date of attachment. If a claim or objection is made, it will be inquired into by the court and may be allowed or disallowed. The claimant's legal representative can continue the claim if they die after the initial filing period.

85.what: If a proclaimed person appears within the time specified, their attached property is released. If they don't appear, the state government can keep it for 6 months or until any claims are resolved. The court may sell it if it's in disrepair or beneficial to the owner. After 2 years, if someone who lost property appears and proves they didn't abscond, their property is returned.

86.what: A person who had an application for restoring attached property rejected can appeal to a higher court if they are unhappy with the decision.

87.what: A Court may issue a warrant for arrest instead of or in addition to a summons if the person has absconded, will not obey the summons, fails to appear after being served with the summons, or no reasonable excuse is given for their absence.

88.what: The officer presiding in any Court may require a person present in such Court to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for their appearance in such Court, or any other Court to which the case may be transferred for trial.

89.what: If someone who has a bond to appear in court doesn't show up, the court can order their arrest.

90.what: The provisions in Chapter VII about summoning people to give evidence apply to all summons and warrants for arrests issued under the Code.

91.what: A court can issue a summons or an officer can give a written order to someone who possesses a document or item needed for an investigation, inquiry, trial, or proceeding. The person must attend and produce it at the specified time and place.

92.what: If any document, parcel or thing in the custody of a postal or telegraph authority is wanted for investigation, inquiry, trial or proceeding, a magistrate can require it to be delivered to a person they direct.

93.what: A Court may issue a search-warrant if it believes a person has information about a document or thing, is avoiding production, or the document/thing is not known to be in someone's possession. The warrant allows for a general search or inspection of a specific place or part.

95.what: The State Government may, by notification, declare every copy of the issue of the newspaper containing such matter, and every copy of such book or other document to be forfeited to Government, and thereupon any police officer may seize the same wherever found in India and any Magistrate may by warrant authorise any police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector to enter upon and search for the same in any premises where any copy of such issue, or any such book or other document may be or may be reasonably suspected to be.

96.what: A person can apply to the High Court within 2 months to set aside a declaration of forfeiture if they believe the publication did not contain objectionable content.

97.what: A District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Magistrate of the first class can issue a search warrant to find a person wrongfully confined if they believe the confinement is an offence.

98.what: A District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or Magistrate of the first class can order the immediate restoration of a woman or female child to her liberty or husband, parent, guardian, or other lawful person, and enforce compliance with the order using necessary force.

99.what: The provisions of sections 38, 70, 72, 74, 77, 78 and 79 apply to all search-warrants issued under sections 93, 94 or 95.

100.what: A person in charge of a closed place must allow an officer to search it on demand and with a warrant. If they refuse, the officer can proceed without them. The officer must inform two independent witnesses before searching. The occupant of the place searched is allowed to attend during the search. Any items seized are listed and signed by the witnesses. Refusing to witness a search can be an offence.

101.what: When, in the execution of a search-warrant at any place beyond the local jurisdiction of the Court which issued the same, any of the things for which search is made, are found, such things, together with the list of the same prepared under the provisions hereinafter contained, shall be immediately taken before the Court issuing the warrant, unless such place is nearer to the Magistrate having jurisdiction therein than to such Court, in which case the list and things shall be immediately taken before such Magistrate; and, unless there be good cause to the contrary, such Magistrate shall make an order authorising them to be taken to such Court.

102.what: A police officer can seize property suspected or alleged to have been stolen, and must report the seizure to a superior officer.

103.what: A Magistrate can order a search in their presence at a location they have the authority to search with a warrant.

104.what: A court can take possession of a document or object that was presented in court.

105.what: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes. Where a Court in the territories to which this Code extends desires that a summons, warrant, or search-warrant be served or executed at any place outside the said territories, it may send such summons or warrant in duplicate by post or otherwise, to the presiding officer of that Court to be served or executed. If the presiding officer has already been served with a summons, the provisions of section 68 apply as if the presiding officer were a Magistrate in the said territories. In cases where arrangements have been made with the Government of a contracting State for service or execution of summons or warrants in relation to criminal matters, the Court may send such summons or warrant in duplicate in a specified form and address, and transmit it to a specified authority.

105B.what: Section 105B states that when a Court in India desires that a warrant for arrest of any person to attend or produce a document or other thing issued by it shall be executed in any place in a contracting State, it shall send such warrant in duplicate in such form to such Court, Judge or Magistrate through such authority, as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf.

105C.what: A court can order the attachment or forfeiture of property if it believes the person who owns it committed an offence and obtained the property from that offence.

105D.what: The Court directs a police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector to trace and identify unlawfully acquired property, including inquiries, investigations, or surveys of persons, places, properties, assets, documents, and financial institutions.

105E.what: Property can be seized or attached if it's likely to be concealed, transferred, or dealt with in a way that will dispose of it.

105F.what: The Court can appoint an administrator to manage properties seized or forfeited, who will receive and manage the property according to government specifications and conditions, and also follow central government directions to dispose of the forfeited property.

105G.what: The Court may serve a notice to a person asking them to explain how they acquired certain properties that are suspected to be proceeds of crime within 30 days.

105H.what: The Court may, after considering the explanation, if any, to the show-cause notice issued under section 105G and the material available before it and after giving to the person affected (and in a case where the person affected holds any property specified in the notice through any other person, to such other person also) a reasonable opportunity of being heard, by order, record a finding whether all or any of the properties in question are proceeds of crime: Provided that if the person affected (and in a case where the person affected holds any property specified in the notice through any other person such other person also) does not appear before the Court or represent his case before it within a period of thirty days specified in the show-cause notice, the Court may proceed to record a finding under this sub-section ex parte on the basis of evidence available before it.

105J.what: If you transfer property after a court order or notice, it will not count for the purpose of the case. If the government later takes possession of that property, the transfer is considered invalid.

105K.what: Every letter of request, summons or warrant received from a contracting State shall be transmitted to the concerned Court in India in the specified form and manner.

105L.what: The Central Government may direct that the application of this Chapter (in relation to a contracting State) is subject to conditions, exceptions or qualifications as specified in a notification.

106.what: When a court convicts someone of certain offenses and thinks it's necessary to keep them from causing trouble, they can order the person to sign a promise to behave for up to 3 years.

107.what: When an Executive Magistrate receives information that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity, he may require such person to show cause why they should not be ordered to execute a bond for keeping the peace for a period not exceeding one year.

108.what: This section states that when an Executive Magistrate receives information about a person disseminating seditious matters, they can require such person to show cause why they should not be ordered to execute a bond for good behaviour for a period not exceeding one year.

109.what: A magistrate can order a suspected person to provide security (a bond) if they believe the person is hiding their presence and may commit a serious crime.

110.what: A magistrate can order a habitual offender to provide security for good behavior if they are involved in serious crimes, including robbery, kidnapping, extortion, and corruption.

111.what: A Magistrate must make a written order stating: what was received, how much bail is needed, for how long it's valid, and if sureties are required.

112.what: If a person present in court does not want to hear the order, the substance of the order will be explained to them instead.

113.what: If a person is not present in court, the magistrate will issue a summons requiring them to appear. If they are in custody, a warrant will be issued directing the officer to bring them before the court. However, if there is reason to fear a breach of peace and immediate arrest is necessary, the magistrate can issue a warrant for their arrest at any time.

114.what: A copy of the order made under section 111 must accompany every summons or warrant issued under section 113. The officer serving or executing the summons or warrant must deliver this copy to the person being served or arrested.

115.what: The Magistrate can decide not to require someone's personal presence if they have a valid reason, and allow them to represent themselves with a lawyer.

116.what: When an order under section 111 has been read or explained under section 112 to a person present in Court, or when any person appears or is brought before a Magistrate in compliance with, or in execution of, a summons or warrant, issued under section 113, the Magistrate shall proceed to inquire into the truth of the information upon which action has been taken, and to take such further evidence as may appear necessary.

117.what: If it's necessary for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour, a Magistrate can order someone to execute a bond with or without sureties. The order must follow these rules: (a) The bond cannot be different from, larger than, or longer than what was specified in section 111. (b) The bond amount must consider the case circumstances and not be excessive. (c) If the person is a minor, only their sureties can execute the bond.

118.what: If an inquiry under section 116 finds that it's not necessary to keep the peace or maintain good behavior, the Magistrate will make a record entry and release the person if they're in custody for the inquiry, or discharge them if they're not.

119.what: If a person is in prison when an order requiring security is made, the time starts after they are released from prison. If not in prison, the time starts on the day the order is made.

120.what: The bond shall bind the person to keep the peace or behave well, and committing an offense that can lead to imprisonment will break the bond.

121.what: A Magistrate can refuse to accept a surety if they believe it's not suitable. The Magistrate must investigate the situation and give notice to the surety and the person who offered them. If the Magistrate finds that the surety is unfit, they can reject them and explain their reasons.

122.what: This section states that if a person ordered to give security does not provide it on time, they will be imprisoned unless there is an exception. The imprisonment period cannot exceed 3 years and can be transferred to another Sessions Judge or Assistant Sessions Judge.

123.what: A District Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate can order the release of a person imprisoned for failing to give security without harming the community. The High Court or Court of Session can also reduce the amount of security, number of sureties, or time required. Conditions imposed on discharge may be cancelled if not fulfilled. If conditions are not fulfilled, the person may be arrested and produced before the District Magistrate. The person must provide security for the unexpired portion of their term to be released. A bond for keeping the peace or good behaviour can be cancelled by the High Court or Court of Session or the District Magistrate.

124.what: A person who appears before a Magistrate or Court after being issued a summons or warrant must give fresh security for the remaining part of their bond.

125.what: Section 125 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the procedure for granting maintenance to a dependent family member. If any person having sufficient means neglects or refuses to maintain their wife, child, father, or mother, who are unable to maintain themselves due to physical or mental abnormalities, injury, or other reasons, a Magistrate of the first class may order such person to make a monthly allowance for the maintenance of the dependent family member. The Magistrate may fix the monthly rate and direct the payment to be made to the dependent family member. Additionally, if the person against whom maintenance is claimed has sufficient income, the Magistrate may also order them to pay the petitioner's expenses during the proceeding. This provision aims to ensure that those who have the means to support their dependents do so, and provides a mechanism for the court to intervene in such cases.

126.what: Proceedings under section 125 may be taken against any person in any district — where he is, or where he or his wife resides, or where he last resided with his wife, or as the case may be, with the mother of the illegitimate child.

127.what: The Magistrate may alter a monthly allowance for maintenance or interim maintenance if there has been a change in circumstances, and cancel an order if a competent Civil Court decision affects it.

128.what: A copy of the order must be given to the person in favour of the order without payment. The order can also be enforced by a Magistrate if they are satisfied that the allowance or expenses have not been paid.

129.what: An Executive Magistrate or police officer can command an unlawful assembly or a group of five or more people likely to disturb public peace to disperse, and it is their duty to do so. If the assembly doesn't disperse, they can use force to disperse it and arrest anyone who refuses to leave.

130.what: Section 130 states that if any assembly cannot be dispersed otherwise, an Executive Magistrate of the highest rank present can cause it to be dispersed by armed forces, and may require officers in command to disperse the assembly with the help of armed forces.

131.what: A commissioned or gazetted officer of the armed forces can disperse an assembly if public security is endangered and no Executive Magistrate can be contacted, but must communicate with a Magistrate if possible.

132.what: No prosecution can be instituted against a person who acted in good faith under sections 129, 130 or 131 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, unless authorized by the Central Government for military personnel or State Government for others.

133.what: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

134.what: The order must be served on the person against whom it is made (if possible) or notified by proclamation with a published notice and posted in a conspicuous place.

135.what: The person against whom such order is made shall— (a) perform, within the time and in the manner specified in the order, the act directed thereby; or (b) appear in accordance with such order and show cause against the same.

136.what: If a person fails to perform an act or appear and show cause, they will be punished with a fine as stated in Section 188 of the Indian Penal Code.

137.what: If an order is made under section 133 to prevent public obstruction, nuisance, or danger, a Magistrate will question the person affected. If they deny public rights, the Magistrate must investigate before proceeding with further action. If no evidence supports their claim, the Magistrate can proceed as usual (section 138). If someone denies public rights but fails to provide evidence, they cannot deny it again in future proceedings.

138.what: If a person who has been ordered to pay money appears and explains why they should not have to, the magistrate will take evidence as if it were a summons case. The order will be made absolute unless the magistrate thinks it is unreasonable or unfair.

139.what: The Magistrate can order a local investigation or summon and examine an expert for the purposes of an inquiry.

140.what: A magistrate can give written instructions to someone conducting a local investigation, decide who pays for expenses, and have their report used as evidence in court.

141.what: The Magistrate must: 1. Notify the person against whom the order was made, and fix a time for them to perform the act. 2. Inform them that disobedience will result in a penalty (section 188 of the Indian Penal Code). 3. If the act is not performed, the Magistrate can cause it to be done and recover costs by selling property or attaching and selling movable assets within their jurisdiction.

142.what: If a Magistrate can take immediate measures to prevent imminent danger, they may issue an injunction to the person against whom the order was made, requiring them to obey. If the person doesn't comply, the Magistrate can take action themselves to prevent harm.

143.what: A District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate, or any other Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government or the District Magistrate in this behalf, may order any person not to repeat or continue a public nuisance, as defined in the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), or any special or local law.

144.what: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger. An order under this section can be directed to a particular individual, persons residing in a place or area, or the public generally. The order may be passed ex parte in emergency situations. It cannot remain in force for more than two months, but it can be extended by notification from the State Government for up to six months.

144A.what: The District Magistrate may prohibit carrying arms in procession or mass drill or mass training with arms in any public place for the preservation of public peace, public safety, or public order.

145.what: Section 145 states that when an Executive Magistrate is satisfied that a dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause a breach of peace, he shall make an order requiring the parties concerned to attend his Court in person or by pleader, on a specified date and time, and to put in written statements of their respective claims as respects the fact of actual possession of the subject of dispute.

146.what: The Magistrate can attach a disputed property if they consider it an emergency, if possession is unclear, or if they're unable to determine who has rightful possession. The Magistrate can also appoint a receiver to manage the property until a court decides on the matter.

147.what: Section 147 states that whenever an Executive Magistrate is satisfied from the report of a police officer or upon other information, that a dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace exists regarding any alleged right of use of any land or water within his local jurisdiction, he shall make an order in writing, stating the grounds of his being so satisfied and requiring the parties concerned in such dispute to attend his Court in person or by pleader on a specified date and time and to put in written statements of their respective claims.

148.what: A District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate can depute a subordinate magistrate to conduct a local inquiry for certain cases, provide written instructions and declare who will pay expenses.

149.what: Police officers have a duty to prevent the commission of cognizable offences.

150.what: If a police officer receives information about a plan to commit a serious crime (cognizable offence), they must: 1) tell their supervisor, and 2) inform another officer who is in charge of stopping or investigating the crime.

151.what: A police officer can arrest someone without a warrant if they think committing a serious crime (cognizable offence) cannot be prevented otherwise.

152.what: A police officer can stop anyone from injuring public property, including buildings, landmarks, and navigation marks, if they witness it.

153.what: An officer in charge of a police station can enter any place within their limits without a warrant to inspect or search for false weights, measures, or instruments used for weighing.

154.what: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, if given orally to an officer in charge of a police station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State Government may prescribe in this behalf:

155.what: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases. When information is given about a non-cognizable offence, an officer must: enter the information in a book; refer the informant to a Magistrate. Police officers cannot investigate these cases without a Magistrate's order. If they receive such an order, they can investigate like they would in a cognizable case (except for arresting without a warrant). If a case involves multiple offences, one of which is cognizable, it is considered cognizable.

156.what: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

157.what: If an officer in charge of a police station has reason to suspect the commission of an offence, he shall forthwith send a report of the same to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of such offence upon a police report and shall proceed in person, or shall depute one of his subordinate officers not being below such rank as the State Government may, by general or special order, prescribe in this behalf, to investigate the facts and circumstances of the case.

158.what: Every report sent to a Magistrate under section 157 must be submitted through a superior officer of police appointed by the State Government, with instructions recorded on the report and transmitted to the Magistrate.

159.what: A magistrate can direct an investigation, proceed immediately, or appoint a lower magistrate to investigate or inquire about a case after receiving a report.

160.what: A police officer can order a witness to attend if they are within their station's limits and appear knowledgeable about the case. The witness must attend, unless they fall into one of these categories: being under 15 or over 65 years old, being female, or having a disability.

161.what: A police officer can examine a person orally about a case, and that person must answer truly, except for questions that could lead to a criminal charge or penalty.

162.what: Section 162 states that no statement made by a person to a police officer during an investigation cannot be signed by the person making it, and such statements cannot be used as evidence unless specifically allowed by law.

163.what: No police officer or other person in authority shall offer or make, or cause to be offered or made, any inducement, threat or promise that may influence a person's statement during an investigation. However, no one can stop someone from making a free will statement during an investigation.

164.what: Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 deals with the recording of confessions and statements made to a Magistrate in the course of an investigation or inquiry.

164A.what: Medical examination of the victim of rape: A woman alleged or attempted to have been raped must be examined by a registered medical practitioner within 24 hours, with her consent or that of a person competent to give consent on her behalf.

165.what: A police officer can search a place if they believe something related to an investigation is there and it's not possible to get it without delay.

166.what: An officer in charge of a police station or a police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector can require another officer to search a place, but only if it's within their own limits. The required officer must follow the same procedures as section 165 and return any found items. If there's reason to believe evidence might be lost, an officer can search the place themselves or have it searched.

166A.what: Section 166A states that if evidence is available in a country or place outside India during an investigation into an offence, a Criminal Court can issue a letter of request to examine a person and record their statement, as well as require them to produce documents or things related to the case.

166B.what: A country or place outside India can send a letter to an Indian court or authority asking for help with investigating an offence. The Indian government will then forward the letter to a magistrate or police officer who will investigate the offence as if it were committed in India.

167.what: Section 167 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 states that any person who intentionally causes disturbance or riot in a public place shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine. This section is often used to prosecute individuals who engage in violent or disorderly behavior in public spaces, such as riots, protests, or other forms of civil unrest.

168.what: When any subordinate police officer has made any investigation under this Chapter, he shall report the result of such investigation to the officer in charge of the police station.

169.what: If, upon an investigation under this Chapter, it appears to the officer in charge of the police station that there is not sufficient evidence or reasonable ground of suspicion to justify the forwarding of the accused to a Magistrate, such officer shall, if such person is in custody, release him on his executing a bond, with or without sureties, as such officer may direct, to appear, if and when so required, before a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence on a police report, and to try the accused or commit him for trial.

170.what: (1) If, upon an investigation under this Chapter, it appears to the officer in charge of the police station that there is sufficient evidence or reasonable ground as aforesaid, such officer shall forward the accused under custody to a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence upon a police report and to try the accused or commit him for trial, or, if the offence is bailable and the accused is able to give security, shall take security from him for his appearance before such Magistrate on a day fixed and for his attendance from day to day before such Magistrate until otherwise directed.

171.what: No complainant or witness on his way to any Court shall be required to accompany a police officer, or shall be subjected to unnecessary restraint or inconvenience, or required to give any security for his appearance other than his own bond: Provided that, if any complainant or witness refuses to attend or to execute a bond as directed in section 170, the officer in charge of the police station may forward him in custody to the Magistrate, who may detain him in custody until he executes such bond, or until the hearing of the case is completed.

172.what: Every police officer making an investigation under this Chapter shall day by day enter his proceedings in the investigation in a diary, setting forth the time at which the information reached him, the time at which he began and closed his investigation, the place or places visited by him, and a statement of the circumstances ascertained through his investigation.

173.what: Every investigation under this Chapter shall be completed without unnecessary delay. The investigation in relation to an offence under sections 376, 376A, 376AB, 376B, 376C, 376D, 376DA, 376DB or 376E from the date on which the information was recorded by the officer in charge of the police station.

174.what: A police officer must report a suicide or suspicious death to the nearest Executive Magistrate, who will then investigate the circumstances of the death. The investigation may involve an autopsy and a report on the cause of death will be prepared and forwarded to the District Magistrate.

175.what: A police officer may, by order in writing, summon two or more persons as aforesaid for the purpose of the said investigation, and any other person who appears to be acquainted with the facts of the case and every person so summoned shall be bound to attend and to answer truly all questions other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture.

176.what: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death: A Magistrate can hold an inquiry into the cause of death instead of or in addition to a police investigation, and has all the powers to conduct it. The Magistrate must inform the relatives of the deceased and allow them to attend the inquiry. If the body is not examined within 24 hours, it must be forwarded to a Civil Surgeon or qualified medical person.

177.what: Every offence shall ordinarily be inquired into and tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed.

178.what: A court can inquire into or try an offence if it was committed partly in one area and another, or if it's a continuing offence that spans multiple areas, or if the offence consists of acts done in different areas.

179.what: An act that is an offence because of something that was done and its consequences can be investigated or tried in a court where the action took place or the consequence occurred.

180.what: If an act is an offence because it relates to another offence, the court where that other offence occurred can try the case.

181.what: Any of the following offences can be tried in a court where the offence occurred or where the accused was found: being a thug, murder committed by a thug, dacoity, dacoity with murder, gang membership, escaping from custody. Kidnapping or abduction can also be tried in a court where the person was kidnapped or abducted. Theft, extortion, robbery, and criminal misappropriation can be tried in a court where the offence occurred or where stolen property was found. Offences involving possession of stolen property can also be tried in a court where the offence occurred or where stolen property was found.

182.what: Offences that can be inquired into or tried by a specific court, including those involving cheating and property delivery, as well as offences under sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code.

183.what: When an offence is committed whilst the person by or against whom, or the thing in respect of which, the offence is committed is in the course of performing a journey or voyage, the offence may be inquired into or tried by a Court through or into whose local jurisdiction that person or thing passed in the course of that journey or voyage.

184.what: Where— (a) the offences committed by any person are such that he may be charged with, and tried at one trial for, each such offence by virtue of the provisions of section 219, section 220 or section 221, or (b) the offence or offences committed by several persons are such that they may be charged with and tried together by virtue of the provisions of section 223, the offences may be inquired into or tried by any Court competent to inquire into or try any of the offences.

185.what: The State Government may direct that any cases or class of cases committed for trial in any district may be tried in any sessions division, provided such direction is not repugnant to any direction previously issued by the High Court or the Supreme Court under the Constitution, or under this Code or any other law for the time being in force.

186.what: If two or more courts take cognizance of the same offense, which court should inquire or try it? If they are subordinate to the same high court, that high court decides. If not, the high court with jurisdiction over the area where the first proceedings started makes the decision, and all other proceedings for that offense stop.

187.what: A Magistrate of the first class can issue a summons or warrant for an offence committed beyond local jurisdiction if they believe it was committed outside their jurisdiction and is triable in India under another law.

188.what: An offence committed outside India can be dealt with as if it were committed at any place within India, but requires the previous sanction of the Central Government to be inquired into or tried in India.

189.what: When any offence alleged to have been committed in a territory outside India is being inquired into or tried under the provisions of section 188, the Central Government may, if it thinks fit, direct that copies of depositions made or exhibits produced before a Judicial officer in or for that territory or before a diplomatic or consular representative of India in or for that territory shall be received as evidence by the Court holding such inquiry or trial in any case in which such Court might issue a commission for taking evidence as to the matters to which such depositions or exhibits relate.

190.what: A magistrate can take cognizance of an offence if they receive a complaint, police report, or information from someone else about the offence.

191.what: Section 191 states that when a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 190, the accused shall be informed that he is entitled to have the case inquired into or tried by another Magistrate, and if the accused objects to further proceedings before the Magistrate taking cognizance, the case shall be transferred to such other Magistrate as may be specified by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

192.what: Section 192 states that any Chief Judicial Magistrate may make over the case for inquiry or trial to any competent Magistrate subordinate to him, and any Magistrate of the first class empowered in this behalf by the Chief Judicial Magistrate may hold the inquiry or trial.

193.what: No Court of Session shall take cognizance of any offence as a Court of original jurisdiction unless the case has been committed to it by a Magistrate under this Code.

194.what: As Additional Sessions Judge or Assistant Sessions Judge shall try such cases as the Sessions Judge of the division may, by general or special order, make over to him for trial or as the High Court may, by special order, direct him to try.

195.what: No Court shall take cognizance of certain offences except on the complaint in writing of the public servant concerned or of some other public servant to whom he is administratively subordinate.

195A.what: A witness or any other person can file a complaint about an offence under this section.

196.what: No Court shall take cognizance of certain offences against the State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such offence, except with the previous sanction of the Central Government or of the State Government or of the District Magistrate.

197.what: Section 197 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 states that no court shall take cognizance of any offence alleged to have been committed by a Judge or public servant except with the previous sanction of the Government, unless the offence is committed in connection with the affairs of the Union or State. Additionally, the provisions of sub-sections (5) and (6) of section 197 apply to all proceedings pending on the date of commencement of this Act in respect of which a Court had taken cognizance of an offence.

198.what: No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under Chapter XX of the Indian Penal Code except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence. Exceptions include: a minor, idiot, lunatic, or woman who cannot appear in public; a husband serving in the Armed Forces with leave denied for making a complaint; or a wife whose complaint can be made on her behalf by certain relatives.

198A.what: No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 498A of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) except upon a police report of facts which constitute such offence or upon a complaint made by the person aggrieved by the offence or by her father, mother, brother, sister or by her father’s or mother’s brother or sister or, with the leave of the Court, by any other person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption.

198B.what: No court can take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 376B of the Indian Penal Code if the persons involved are in a marital relationship, except if the wife files a complaint.

199.what: No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under Chapter XXI of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence: Provided that where such person is under the age of eighteen years, or is an idiot or a lunatic, or is from sickness or infirmity unable to make a complaint, or is a woman who, according to the local customs, ought not to be compelled to appear in public, some other person may, with the leave of the Court, make a complaint on her behalf.

200.what: A Magistrate must examine a person who files a complaint on oath, along with any present witnesses. The examination's substance will be written down and signed by all parties involved.

201.what: If the complaint is made to a Magistrate who is not competent to take cognizance of the offence, he shall return it for presentation to the proper Court with an endorsement to that effect; if the complaint is not in writing, direct the complainant to the proper Court.

202.what: The Magistrate may postpone the issue of process against the accused and either inquire into the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by a police officer or another person, if there is sufficient ground for proceeding.

203.what: If, after considering the statements on oath (if any) of the complainant and of the witnesses and the result of the inquiry or investigation (if any) under section 202, the Magistrate is of opinion that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, he shall dismiss the complaint, and in every such case he shall briefly record his reasons for so doing.

205.what: A Magistrate may dispense with the personal attendance of an accused and permit him to appear by his pleader, but the Magistrate inquiring into or trying the case may direct the personal attendance of the accused and enforce such attendance if necessary.

206.what: A Magistrate can issue a summons to an accused in a petty offence case, requiring them to appear or plead guilty by mail, with certain conditions.

207.what: Section 207 states that in any case where the proceeding has been instituted on a police report, the Magistrate shall without delay furnish to the accused, free of cost, a copy of each of the following documents: the police report, first information report recorded under section 154, statements recorded under sub-section (3) of section 161, confessions and statements recorded under section 164, and any other document or relevant extract thereof forwarded to the Magistrate with the police report.

208.what: The Magistrate must provide the accused with free copies of statements and documents if the case is triable exclusively by the Court of Session.

209.what: Section 209 states that when an offence is triable exclusively by the Court of Session, the Magistrate shall commit the case to the Court of Session and remand the accused to custody until such commitment has been made.

210.what: When a complaint case and police investigation are happening for the same offence, the Magistrate must stop the case, get a report from the police officer, and then decide whether to try both cases together or continue with just one.

211.what: Every charge under this Code shall state the offence with which the accused is charged, including the law and section of the law against which the offence is said to have been committed.

212.what: The charge must contain specific details about the time, place, person, or thing involved in the alleged offense, so the accused can understand what they are being charged with.

213.what: When the nature of the case is such that the particulars mentioned in sections 211 and 212 do not give the accused sufficient notice of the matter with which he is charged, the charge shall also contain such particulars of the manner in which the alleged offence was committed as will be sufficient for that purpose.

214.what: In every charge words used in describing an offence shall be deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them respectively by the law under which such offence is punishable.

215.what: This section states that no error in stating either the offence or the particulars required to be stated in the charge, and no omission to state the offence or those particulars, shall be regarded at any stage of the case as material, unless the accused was in fact misled by such error or omission, and it has occasioned a failure of justice.

216.what: This section states that any Court may alter or add to any charge at any time before judgment is pronounced, with certain conditions and procedures applied to ensure fairness and protection for the accused and prosecutor.

217.what: Whenever a charge is altered or added to by the Court after the commencement of the trial, the prosecutor and the accused shall be allowed to recall or re-summon, and examine with reference to such alteration or addition, any witness who may have been examined, unless the Court considers that this is done for vexation or delay or to defeat justice.

218.what: For every distinct offence of which any person is accused there shall be a separate charge, and every such charge shall be tried separately: Provided that where the accused person, by an application in writing, so desires and the Magistrate is of opinion that such person is not likely to be prejudiced thereby, the Magistrate may try together all or any number of the charges framed against such person.

219.what: Three offences of the same kind committed within a year may be charged together, with a limit of three offences in total.

220.what: Section 220 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains that in cases where multiple offences are committed by the same person as part of the same transaction, they can be charged and tried together in a single trial for every such offence. However, if several acts combine to form different offences, the accused may be tried only once for each separate offence. This provision allows for the simultaneous trial of related offences, streamlining the legal process and reducing the burden on the court.

221.what: If a single act or series of acts is of such a nature that it is doubtful which of several offences the facts which can be proved will constitute, the accused may be charged with having committed all or any of such offences, and any number of such charges may be tried at once; or he may be charged in the alternative with having committed some one of the said offences.

222.what: When a person can be convicted of a lesser offence if some but not all of the charged offence's particulars are proved, or if the facts prove the offence is less serious than charged.

223.what: The following persons may be charged and tried together: (a) those accused of the same offence in the same transaction; (b) those accused of an offence and abetment or attempt to commit it; (c) those accused of multiple offences of the same kind committed jointly within 12 months; (d) those accused of different offences in the same transaction; (e) those accused of theft, extortion, etc. and related crimes such as receiving stolen property or assisting in its disposal; (f) those accused of offences under sections 411 and 414 of the Indian Penal Code relating to stolen property; (g) those accused of counterfeit coin-related offences and other similar offences, with provisions from Chapter XII of the Indian Penal Code applying where applicable.

224.what: When a charge containing more heads than one is framed against the same person, and when a conviction has been had on one or more of them, the complainant, or the officer conducting the prosecution, may, with the consent of the Court, withdraw the remaining charge or charges, or the Court of its own accord may stay the inquiry into, or trial of, such charge or charges and such withdrawal shall have the effect of an acquittal on such charge or charges, unless the conviction be set aside, in which case the said Court (subject to the order of the Court setting aside the conviction) may proceed with the inquiry into, or trial of, the charge or charges so withdrawn.

225.what: In every trial before a Court of Session, the prosecution shall be conducted by a Public Prosecutor.

226.what: When the accused appears or is brought before the Court i n pursuance of a commitment of the case under section 209, the prosecutor shall open his case by describing the charge brought against the accused and stating by what evidence he proposes to prove the guilt of the accused.

227.what: If, upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith, and after hearing the submissions of the accused and the prosecution in this behalf, the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.

228.what: The Judge may frame a charge against the accused and transfer the case for trial to a Chief Judicial Magistrate or any other Judicial Magistrate of the first class if the accused has committed an offence that is not exclusively triable by the Court of Session, or frame a written charge against the accused if it is exclusively triable by the Court. The charge must be read and explained to the accused, who can then plead guilty or claim to be tried.

229.what: If the accused pleads guilty, the Judge shall record the plea and may, in his discretion, convict him thereon.

230.what: If the accused refuses to plead, or does not plead, or claims to be tried or is not convicted under section 229, the Judge shall fix a date for the examination of witnesses, and may, on the application of the prosecution, issue any process for compelling the attendance of any witness or the production of any document or other thing.

231.what: The Judge shall proceed to take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution on a fixed date, and may permit cross-examination to be deferred or recall any witness for further cross-examination.

232.what: If the Judge finds no evidence that the accused committed the offence after taking the evidence for the prosecution, examining the accused, and hearing both the prosecution and defence, the Judge shall record an order of acquittal.

233.what: The accused is called upon to enter on his defence and adduce any evidence he may have in support thereof, and if he puts in a written statement, it shall be filed with the record.

234.what: When the examination of witnesses for the defence is complete, the prosecutor sums up his case, and the accused or his pleader is entitled to reply, with permission from the Judge to make submissions on any point of law raised by the accused.

235.what: Section 235 states that after hearing arguments and points of law, the Judge shall give a judgment in the case. If the accused is convicted, the Judge shall hear the accused on the questions of sentence and then pass sentence according to law.

236.what: Section 236 states that if a previous conviction is charged under certain provisions, the Judge may take evidence in respect of the alleged previous conviction after convicting the accused under sections 229 or 235, but only if the accused has been convicted under those sections.

237.what: A Court of Session taking cognizance of an offence under sub-section (2) of section 199 shall try the case in accordance with the procedure for the trial of warrant-cases instituted otherwise than on a police report before a Court of Magistrate: Provided that the person against whom the offence is alleged to have been committed shall, unless the Court of Session, for reasons to be recorded, otherwise directs, be examined as a witness for the prosecution.

238.what: The Magistrate must ensure the accused complies with Section 207 when appearing in court.

239.what: If, upon considering the police report and the documents sent with it under section 173 and making such examination, if any, of the accused as the Magistrate thinks necessary and after giving the prosecution and the accused an opportunity of being heard, the Magistrate considers the charge against the accused to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused, and record his reasons for so doing.

240.what: STATE AMENDMENT Chhattisgarh In sub-section ( 2) of section 240 of the Principal Act, after the word “to the accused” the following shall be added:— “present either in person or through the medium of electronic video linkage in the presence of his pleader in the Court.” [Vide Chhattisgarh Act 13 of 2006, s. 5].

241.what: If the accused pleads guilty, the Magistrate shall record the plea and may, in his discretion, convict him thereon.

242.what: (1) If the accused refuses to plead or does not plead, or claims to be tried or the Magistrate does not convict the accused under section 241, the Magistrate shall fix a date for the examination of witnesses: 1[Provided that the Magistrate shall supply in advance to the accused, the statement of witnesses recorded during investigation by the police]. (2) The Magistrate may, on the application of the prosecution, issue a summons to any of its witnesses directing him to attend or to produce any document or other thing. (3) On the date so fixed, the Magistrate shall proceed to take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution: Provided that the Magistrate may permit the cross-examination of any witness to be deferred until any other witness or witnesses have been examined or recall any witness for further cross-examination.

243.what: The accused shall then be called upon to enter upon his defence and produce his evidence; and if the accused puts in any written statement, the Magistrate shall file it with the record.

244.what: When, in any warrant-case instituted otherwise than on a police report, the accused appears or is brought before a Magistrate, the Magistrate shall proceed to hear the prosecution and take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution.

245.what: Section 245 states that if a Magistrate considers that no case against an accused has been made out which would warrant conviction, the Magistrate shall discharge the accused, unless the prosecution satisfies the Magistrate that it is not in the interest of justice to do so.

246.what: If a Magistrate thinks the accused has committed an offence that can be tried by them and punished adequately, they must frame a written charge against the accused. The charge is then read to the accused, who can plead guilty or make a defence. If the accused pleads guilty, the Magistrate may convict them. If not, the accused must state which witnesses they want to cross-examine at the next hearing.

247.what: The accused must defend themselves and present their own evidence, with the rules from section 243 applying.

248.what: (1) If, in any case under this Chapter in which a charge has been framed, the Magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall record an order of acquittal. (2) Where, in any case under this Chapter, the Magistrate finds the accused guilty, but does not proceed in accordance with the provisions of section 325 or section 360, he shall, after hearing the accused on the question of sentence, pass sentence upon him according to law. (3) Where, in any case under this Chapter, a previous conviction is charged under the provisions o f sub-section (7) of section 211 and the accused does not admit that he has been previously convicted as alleged in the charge, the Magistrate may, after he has convicted the said accused, take evidence in respect of the alleged previous conviction, and shall record a finding thereon: Provided that no such charge shall be read out by the Magistrate nor shall the accused be asked to plead thereto nor shall the previous conviction be referred to by the prosecution or in any evidence adduced by it, unless and until the accused has been convicted under sub-section (2).

249.what: When the proceedings have been instituted upon complaint, and on any day fixed for the hearing of the case, the complainant is absent, and the offence may be lawfully compounded or is not a cognizable offence, the Magistrate may, in his discretion, notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained, at any time before the charge has been framed, discharge the accused.

250.what: If, in any case instituted upon complaint or upon information given to a police officer or to a Magistrate, one or more persons is or are accused before a Magistrate of any offence triable by a Magistrate, and the Magistrate by whom the case is heard discharges or acquits all or any of the accused, and is of opinion that there was no reasonable ground for making the accusation against them or any of them, the Magistrate may, by his order of discharge or acquittal, if the person upon whose complaint or information the accusation was made is present, call upon him forthwith to show cause why he should not pay compensation to such accused or to each or any of such accused when there are more than one; or, if such person is not present, direct the issue of a summons to him to appear and show cause as aforesaid.

251.what: When in a summons-case the accused appears or is brought before the Magistrate, the particulars of the offence of which he is accused shall be stated to him, and he shall be asked whether he pleads guilty or has any defence to make, but it shall not be necessary to frame a formal charge.

252.what: If the accused pleas guilty, the Magistrate will write down their words exactly or change them slightly to make sense, then convict them.

253.what: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases: The accused shall transmit to the Magistrate a letter containing his plea and the amount of fine specified in the summons, and the Magistrate may convict the accused in his absence, on his plea of guilty and sentence him to pay the fine.

254.what: Procedure when not convicted: If the Magistrate does not convict the accused under section 252 or section 253, he shall proceed to hear the prosecution and take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution, and also to hear the accused and take all such evidence as he produces in his defence.

255.what: If the Magistrate finds the accused not guilty, he shall record an order of acquittal. If the Magistrate finds the accused guilty, he shall pass sentence upon him according to law.

256.what: If a person who has filed a complaint does not appear in court on the appointed day or any subsequent day, the Magistrate will acquit the accused unless it's deemed necessary to adjourn the hearing. The Magistrate can decide not to require the complainant's attendance if they are represented by someone else or if their presence is not needed.

257.what: If a complainant, at any time before a final order is passed in any case under this Chapter, satisfies the Magistrate that there are sufficient grounds for permitting him to withdraw his complaint against the accused, or if there be more than one accused, against all or any of them, the Magistrate may permit him to withdraw the same, and shall thereupon acquit the accused against whom the complaint is so withdrawn.
