258.what: In any summons-case instituted otherwise than upon complaint, a Magistrate of the first class or, with the previous sanction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, any other Judicial Magistrate, may, for reasons to be recorded by him, stop the proceedings at any stage without pronouncing any judgment and where such stoppage of proceedings is made after the evidence of the principal witnesses has been recorded, pronounce a judgment of acquittal, and in any other case, release the accused, and such release shall have the effect of discharge.

259.what: The Magistrate may proceed to re-hear a summons-case relating to an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months, in accordance with the procedure for the trial of warrant-cases, and may re-call any witness who may have been examined.

260.what: A Chief Judicial Magistrate, Metropolitan Magistrate, or a specially empowered Magistrate can try certain offences summarily if they think it's appropriate, including: theft with property value under 2000 rupees, receiving stolen property, assisting in concealing stolen property, and certain other crimes.

261.what: The High Court may confer on any Magistrate invested with the powers of a Magistrate of the second class power to try summarily any offence which is punishable only with fine or with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months with or without fine, and any abetment of or attempt to commit any such offence.

262.what: In trials under this Chapter, the procedure specified in this Code for the trial of summons-case shall be followed except as hereinafter mentioned. No sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding three months shall be passed in the case of any conviction under this Chapter.

263.what: In every case tried summarily, the Magistrate shall enter, in such form as the State Government may direct, the following particulars, namely:— (a) the serial number of the case; (b) the date of the commission of the offence; (c) the date of the report or complaint; (d) the name of the complainant (if any); (e) the name, parentage and residence of the accused; (f) the offence complained of and the offence (if any) proved, and in cases coming under clause (ii), clause (iii) or clause (iv) of s ub-section (1) of section 260, the value of the property in respect of which the offence has been committed; (g) the plea of the accused and his examination (if any); (h) the finding; (i) the sentence or other final order; (j) the date on which proceedings terminated.

264.what: The Magistrate shall record the substance of the evidence and a judgment containing a brief statement of the reasons for the finding.

265.what: Every record and judgment shall be written in the language of the Court. The High Court may authorise any Magistrate to prepare the record or judgment by means of an officer appointed in this behalf by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and the record or judgment so prepared shall be signed by such Magistrate.

265A.what: This Chapter applies in respect of an accused against whom a report has been forwarded alleging an offence other than one for which the punishment of death or imprisonment for life or exceeding seven years has been provided under the law, and does not apply where the offence affects the socio-economic condition of the country or has been committed against a woman or child below 14 years.

265B.what: A person accused of an offence may file an application for plea bargaining in the Court in which such offence is pending for trial.

265C.what: The Court shall follow a specific procedure when working out a mutually satisfactory disposition under section 265B: In cases instituted on police report, all parties must attend a meeting. In other cases, only the accused and victim must attend a meeting.

265D.what: Where in a meeting under section 265C, a satisfactory disposition of the case has been worked out, the Court shall prepare a report of such disposition which shall be signed by the presiding officer of the Court and all other persons who participated in the meeting and if no such disposition has been worked out, the Court shall record such observation and proceed further in accordance with the provisions of this Code from the stage the application under sub-section (1) of section 265B has been filed in such case.

265E.what: The Court shall dispose of the case by awarding compensation to the victim and hearing parties on punishment, probation, or release, following specific procedures.

265F.what: The Court shall deliver its judgment in terms of section 265E in the open Court and the same shall be signed by the presiding officer of the Court.

265G.what: The judgment delivered by the Court is final, with no appeals allowed except for certain petitions.

265H.what: A Court shall have, for the purposes of discharging its functions under this Chapter, all the powers vested in respect of bail, trial of offences and other matters relating to the disposal of a case in such Court under this Code.

265J.what: The provisions of this Chapter shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other provisions of this Code and nothing in such other provisions shall be construed to constrain the meaning of any provision of this Chapter.

265K.what: Notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, the statements or facts stated by an accused in an application for plea bargaining filed under section 265B shall not be used for any other purpose except for the purpose of this Chapter.

265L.what: Nothing in this Chapter applies to juveniles or children as defined in clause (k) of section 2 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000.

266.what: This Chapter defines key terms such as 'detained' and 'prison', including subsidiary jails and reformatory institutions.

268.what: The State Government has the power to exclude certain persons from the operation of section 267 by issuing a general or special order.

269.what: The officer in charge of a prison must not carry out an order if the person is: sick/infirm, under trial/remand, or will be released before the order can be carried out. If this happens, they must send a statement to the court explaining why.

270.what: The officer in charge of the prison must bring the prisoner to court in custody and keep them there until they are examined or released back to prison

271.what: The provisions of this Chapter shall be without prejudice to the power of the Court to issue, under section 284, a commission for the examination, as a witness, of any person confined or detained in a prison; and the provisions of Part B of Chapter XXIII shall apply in relation to the examination on commission of any such person in the prison as they apply in relation to the examination on commission of any other person.

272.what: The State Government may determine what shall be, for purposes of this Code, the language of each Court within the State other than the High Court.

273.what: All evidence taken in the course of a trial or other proceeding must be taken in the presence of the accused, or with their pleader present, unless otherwise expressly provided.

274.what: The Magistrate must make a written record of the evidence presented during a summons-case, inquiry, or other proceedings, unless they are unable to do so themselves.

275.what: In all warrant-cases tried before a Magistrate, the evidence of each witness shall, as his examination proceeds, be taken down in writing either by the Magistrate himself or by his dictation in open Court or, where he is unable to do so owing to a physical or other incapacity, under his direction and superintendence, by an officer of the Court appointed by him in this behalf.

276.what: The evidence of each witness shall be taken down in writing by the presiding Judge or his dictation, or under his direction and superintendence by an officer of the Court.

277.what: In every case where evidence is taken down under section 275 or 276,— (a) if the witness gives evidence in the language of the Court, it shall be taken down in that language; (b) if he gives evidence in any other language, it may, if practicable, be taken down in that language, and if it is not practicable to do so, a true translation of the evidence in the language of the Court shall be prepared as the examination of the witness proceeds, signed by the Magistrate or presiding Judge, and shall form part of the record; (c) where under clause (b) evidence is taken down in a language other than the language of the Court, a true translation thereof in the language of the Court shall be prepared as soon as practicable, signed by the Magistrate or presiding Judge, and shall form part of the record: Provided that when under clause ( b) evidence is taken down in English and a translation thereof in the language of the Court is not required by any of the parties, the Court may dispense with such translation.

278.what: The evidence of each witness taken under sections 275 or 276 shall be read over to the accused in attendance or his pleader if he appears by pleader, and may be corrected if necessary. If a witness objects to any part of the evidence, the Magistrate or Judge may make a memorandum of the objection and add remarks as needed. If the record is in a language different from the one given, it shall be interpreted for the witness in that language or a language they understand.

279.what: Whenever any evidence is given in a language not understood by the accused, and he is present in Court in person, it shall be interpreted to him in open Court in a language understood by him. If he appears by pleader and the evidence is given in a language other than the language of the Court, and not understood by the pleader, it shall be interpreted to such pleader in that language. When documents are put for the purpose of formal proof, it shall be in the discretion of the Court to interpret as much thereof as appears necessary.

280.what: When a presiding Judge or Magistrate has recorded the evidence of a witness, he shall also record such remarks (if any) as he thinks material respecting the demeanour of such witness whilst under examination.

281.what: Section 281 states that when an accused is examined by a Metropolitan Magistrate, the Magistrate must make a memorandum of the examination in the language of the Court and sign it, which shall form part of the record. When an accused is examined by any other Magistrate or Court, the whole examination must be recorded in full by the presiding Judge or Magistrate, who may appoint an officer to assist with recording if needed.

282.what: An interpreter must accurately convey the meaning of evidence or statements in court.

283.what: Every High Court may prescribe a rule for taking down evidence of witnesses and examining the accused.

284.what: Whenever, in the course of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code, it appears to a Court or Magistrate that the examination of a witness is necessary for the ends of justice, and that the attendance of such witness cannot be procured without an amount of delay, expense or inconvenience which, under the circumstances of the case, would be unreasonable, the Court or Magistrate may dispense with such attendance and may issue a commission for the examination of the witness in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter: Provided that where the examination of the President or the Vice-President of India or the Governor of a State or the Administrator of a Union territory as a witness is necessary for the ends of Justice, a commission shall be issued for the examination of such a witness. (2) The Court may, when issuing a commission for the examination of a witness for the prosecution, direct that such amount as the Court considers reasonable to meet the expenses of the accused, including the pleader's fees, be paid by the prosecution.

285.what: The commission shall be directed to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or the Chief Judicial Magistrate, as the case may be, within whose local jurisdiction the witness is to be found if the witness is within the territories to which this Code extends. If the witness is in India, but in a State or an area to which this Code does not extend, the commission shall be directed to such Court or officer as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf.

286.what: The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, or Chief Judicial Magistrate, or a designated Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate, must summon a witness before them or visit their location to take their evidence, exercising the same powers as during trials or warrant cases.

287.what: Parties to a proceeding can ask questions of witnesses in writing, and the court or magistrate can then ask those questions to the witness.

288.what: A commission issued under section 284 must be returned to the Court or Magistrate issuing it, along with the witness's deposition, which can be inspected and read in evidence at any time

289.what: In every case in which a commission is issued under section 284, the inquiry, trial or other proceeding may be adjourned for a specified time reasonably sufficient for the execution and return of the commission.

290.what: The provisions of section 286 and so much of section 287 and section 288 as relate to the execution of a commission and its return shall apply in respect of commissions issued by any of the Courts, Judges or Magistrates hereinafter mentioned as they apply to commissions issued under section 284.

291.what: This section states that the deposition of a medical witness can be given in evidence in any inquiry, trial, or other proceeding under this Code, even if the deponent is not called as a witness.

291A.what: Any document purporting to be a report of identification under an Executive Magistrate's hand can be used as evidence in court proceedings, but certain statements may not be admissible without following specific Indian Evidence Act provisions.

292.what: Any document purporting to be a report under the hand of an officer of the Mint or of any Note Printing Press or of any Security Printing Press (including the officer of the Controller of Stamps and Stationery) or of any Forensic Department or Division of Forensic Science Laboratory or any Government Examiner of Questioned Documents or any State Examiner of Questioned Documents, as the case may be, upon any matter or thing duly submitted to him for examination and report in the course of any proceeding under this Code, may be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code, although such officer is not called as a witness.

293.what: A document from a government scientific expert's report can be used as evidence in court proceedings if it was submitted for examination and analysis.

294.what: Section 294 states that when a document is filed before any court, the prosecution or accused must admit or deny the genuineness of each document, and the list of documents shall be in a form prescribed by the State Government.

295.what: Section 295 allows public servants to give evidence of facts alleged in an application by affidavit, and the court may order that such evidence be given if it thinks fit.

296.what: The evidence of any person whose evidence is of a formal character may be given by affidavit and may, subject to all just exceptions, be read in evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under this Code.

297.what: Affidavits to be used before any Court under this Code may be sworn or affirmed before any Judge or Judicial or Executive Magistrate, or any Commissioner of Oaths appointed by a High Court or Court of Session, or any notary appointed under the Notaries Act, 1952.

298.what: A previous conviction or acquittal may be proved in an inquiry, trial, or other proceeding under this Code by an extract certified under the hand of the officer having the custody of the records of the Court in which such conviction or acquittal was held, or by a certificate signed by the officer in charge of the Jail in which the punishment or any part thereof was undergone.

299.what: If an accused person absconding is to be tried, the court may examine witnesses produced on behalf of the prosecution and record their depositions, which can be given in evidence against the accused if the witness is dead, incapable, or cannot be found without unreasonable delay, expense, or inconvenience.

300.what: A person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence, nor on the same facts for any other offence for which a different charge from the one made against him might have been made under sub-section (1) of section 221, or for which he might have been convicted under sub-section (2) thereof.

301.what: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of a case may appear and plead without any written authority before any Court in which that case is under inquiry, trial or appeal.

302.what: Any Magistrate inquiring into or trying a case may permit the prosecution to be conducted by any person other than a police officer below the rank of inspector; but no person, other than the Advocate-General or Government Advocate or a Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor, shall be entitled to do so without such permission.

303.what: Any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court, or against whom proceedings are instituted under this Code, may of right be defended by a pleader of his choice.

304.what: (1) Where, in a trial before the Court of Session, the accused is not represented by a pleader, and where it appears to the Court that the accused has not sufficient means to engage a pleader, the Court shall assign a pleader for his defence at the expense of the State. (2) The High Court may, with the previous approval of the State Government, make rules providing for— (a) the mode of selecting pleaders for defence under sub-section (1); (b) the facilities to be allowed to such pleaders by the Courts; (c) the fees payable to such pleaders by the Government, and generally, for carrying out the purposes of sub-section (1). (3) The State Government may, by notification, direct that, as from such date as may be specified in the notification, the provisions of sub-sections (1) and (2) shall apply in relation to any class of trials before other Courts in the State as they apply in relation to trials before Courts of Session.

305.what: This section outlines the procedure for corporations and registered societies when they are accused in an inquiry or trial, including the appointment of representatives and the application of certain requirements to these representatives.

306.what: This section states that with a view to obtaining the evidence of any person supposed to have been directly or indirectly concerned in or privy to an offence to which this section applies, the Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Metropolitan Magistrate at any stage of the investigation or inquiry into, or the trial of, the offence, and the Magistrate of the first class inquiring into or trying the offence, at any stage of the inquiry or trial, may tender a pardon to such person on condition of his making a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relative to the offence and to every other person concerned, whether as principal or abettor, in the commission thereof.

307.what: The Court can offer a pardon to someone who has been committed for an offense before judgment is passed, with the goal of getting them to testify at trial about their involvement in the crime.

308.what: Section 308 states that a person who has accepted a tender of pardon may be tried for the offence in respect of which the pardon was made or for any other offence of which they appear to have been guilty in connection with the same matter, and also for the offence of giving false evidence.

309.what:
Section 309 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the procedure for postponing or adjourning court proceedings. Key aspects include: 

- The Court may postpone or adjourn proceedings from day-to-day until all witnesses are examined unless it finds adjournment necessary for reasons to be recorded.

- In cases related to certain offenses (sections 376, 376A, 376B, 376C, 376D, 376DA, and 376DB of the Indian Penal Code), proceedings must be completed within two months from the date of filing the charge sheet.

- The Court can postpone or adjourn proceedings for reasons to be recorded, with reasonable terms and time.

- No Magistrate can remand an accused person to custody for more than 15 days at a time.

- Adjournments are not granted without examining witnesses unless special reasons are recorded in writing.

- No adjournment is allowed solely to enable the accused to show cause against the proposed sentence.

- Adjournments are not granted at the request of a party except in exceptional circumstances, such as the witness being engaged in another court or the party's pleader being unavailable.

- The Court may record the statement of a witness if they are present but the party or their pleader is not ready to examine or cross-examine them.

- The court may postpone or adjourn proceedings for a maximum period of six months from the date of filing of the charge sheet.

310.what: A Judge or Magistrate may visit and inspect any place relevant to an inquiry or trial, recording a memorandum of facts observed, which forms part of the case record.

311.what: A Court can summon or examine any person present, including those not summoned as witnesses, if their evidence is deemed essential for the case's just decision.

311A.what: A Magistrate of the first class may direct a person to give specimen signatures or handwriting if it is expedient for an investigation or proceeding under this Code, and the person has been arrested in connection with such investigation or proceeding.

312.what: A Criminal Court may order payment of reasonable expenses of complainants or witnesses attending for purposes of inquiry, trial, or other proceedings under this Code, subject to rules made by the State Government.

313.what: The court may put questions to the accused at any stage without warning, and shall question him generally on the case after the prosecution witnesses have been examined, except in summons cases where personal attendance is dispensed with.

314.what: A party can give oral arguments and submit a written memorandum after presenting evidence, which must be part of the record. The opposing party must receive a copy of the written memorandum. The Court may delay filing written arguments if it deems them unnecessary.

315.what: Any person accused of an offence before a Criminal Court shall be a competent witness for the defence and may give evidence on oath in disproof of the charges made against him or any person charged together with him at the same trial, provided that he shall not be called as a witness except on his own request in writing.

316.what: No one can use promises, threats, or other means to get a person who is accused of a crime to tell more or less than they know about the case.

317.what: Section 317 states that a Judge or Magistrate may dispense with the personal attendance of an accused in certain cases if they are satisfied that it is not necessary for justice, and may direct their attendance at any subsequent stage of proceedings.

318.what: Section 318 outlines the procedure to be followed when an accused cannot understand the proceedings, allowing the Court to proceed with the inquiry or trial and forwarding the case to a High Court if necessary.

319.what: The court can proceed against other persons appearing guilty of an offence, and they can be arrested or summoned based on the circumstances of the case.

320.what: Section 320 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the compounding of offences. According to this section, a person can compound certain offences with the permission of a court, except in cases where the accused is under 18 years old, an idiot, or a lunatic. The legal representative of a deceased person can also compound the offence with the consent of the court. In other cases, composition for the offence is allowed only if the accused has not been committed for trial or convicted and an appeal is pending. A High Court or Court of Session can allow a person to compound an offence if they are competent to do so under this section. The composition of an offence has the effect of an acquittal for the accused. No offence can be compounded if the accused is liable for enhanced punishment or a different kind of punishment due to a previous conviction.

321.what: The Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of a case may withdraw from the prosecution of any person either generally or in respect of one or more offences with the consent of the Court before judgment is pronounced, and upon such withdrawal, the accused shall be discharged or acquitted depending on whether a charge has been framed or not.

322.what: If a Magistrate appears to warrant a presumption that he lacks jurisdiction to try a case or commit it for trial, he may stay proceedings and submit the case to a higher authority with jurisdiction, who can then decide whether to try the case themselves or refer it to another Magistrate.

323.what: If a Magistrate finds that a case should be tried by the Court of Session, they will transfer it to that court and follow the rules for transferring cases.

324.what: Where a person, having been convicted of an offence punishable under Chapter XII or Chapter XVII of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), with imprisonment for a term of three years or upwards, is again accused of any offence punishable under either of those Chapters with imprisonment for a term of three years or upwards, and

325.what: Whenever a Magistrate is of opinion, after hearing the evidence for the prosecution and the accused, that the accused is guilty, and that he ought to receive a punishment different in kind from, or more severe than, that which such Magistrate is empowered to inflict, or, being a Magistrate of the second class, is of opinion that the accused ought to be required to execute a bond under section 106, he may record the opinion and submit his proceedings, and forward the accused, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate to whom he is subordinate.

326.what: When a case is transferred, the new judge/magistrate can act on previously recorded evidence from the previous judge/magistrate, but may re-examine witnesses if necessary.

327.what: The place in which any Criminal Court is held for the purpose of inquiring into or trying any offence shall be deemed to be an open Court, to which the public generally may have access, so far as the same can conveniently contain them: Provided that the presiding Judge or Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, order at any stage of any inquiry into, or trial of, any particular case, that the public generally, or any particular person, shall not have access to, or be or remain in, the room or building used by the Court.

328.what: This section deals with the procedure to be followed when a magistrate holds an inquiry into the case of an accused who is believed to be of unsound mind and incapable of making their defense.

329.what: Section 329 states that if a person is tried before a Magistrate or Court of Session and appears to be of unsound mind, the court shall try the fact of such unsoundness and incapacity, record a finding, and postpone further proceedings in the case. If the accused is found to be of unsound mind, they will be referred to a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist for care and treatment.

330.what: This section states that whenever a person found under sections 328 or 329 to be incapable of entering defense by reason of unsoundness of mind or mental retardation, the Magistrate or Court may order release on bail, provided certain conditions are met.

331.what: The Magistrate or Court can resume an inquiry or trial at any time after a person has regained sound mind, and require the accused to appear.

332.what: If an accused appears or is brought before a Magistrate or Court, the inquiry or trial will proceed if they are capable of making their defence. If not, the court must act according to sections 328 or 329 and deal with the accused as per section 330 if they are found to be of unsound mind.

333.what: If an accused appears to be of sound mind at the time of inquiry or trial, and there is reason to believe they committed an act that would have been an offence if they were sane, but were incapable due to unsoundness of mind, the Magistrate will proceed with the case and commit them for trial before the Court of Session.

334.what: Whenever any person is acquitted upon the ground that, at the time at which he is alleged to have committed an offence, he was, by reason of unsoundness of mind, incapable of knowing the nature of the act alleged as constituting the offence, or that it was wrong or contrary to law, the finding shall state specifically whether he committed the act or not.

335.what: Whenever the finding states that the accused person committed the act alleged, the Magistrate or Court before whom or which the trial has been held, shall, if such act would, but for the incapacity found, have constituted an offence,— (a) order such person to be detained in safe custody in such place and manner as the Magistrate or Court thinks fit; or (b) order such person to be delivered to any relative or friend of such person.

336.what: The State Government may empower the officer in charge of the jail in which a person is confined under the provisions of section 330 or section 335 to discharge all or any of the functions of the Inspector-General of Prisons under section 337 or section 338.

337.what: If such person is detained under the provisions of sub-section ( 2) of section 330, and in the case of a person detained in a jail, th e Inspector-General of Prisons, or, in the case of a person detained a lunatic asylum, the visitors of such asylum, or any two of them shall certify that, in his or their opinion, such person is capable of making his defence, he shall be taken before the Magistrate or Court, as the case may be, at such time as the Magistrate or Court appoints, and the Magistrate or Court shall deal with such person under the provisions of section 332; and the certificate of such Inspector-General or visitors as aforesaid shall be receivable as evidence.

338.what: This section states that if a person detained under certain provisions is declared fit to be released, the State Government may order their release or detention in custody, or transfer them to a public lunatic asylum. In case of transfer, a Commission consisting of a Judicial and two medical officers can be appointed to make a formal inquiry into the state of mind of such person.

339.what: This section states that if any relative or friend of a detained person applies for their delivery to their care and custody, the State Government may order their release under certain conditions, including giving security to ensure proper care and prevention of injury to themselves or others. The delivered person must be produced for inspection at specified times and places.

340.what: Section 340 states that when a court is of opinion that it is expedient in the interests of justice to make an inquiry into an offence referred to in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 195, it may record a finding, make a complaint, send it to a magistrate, take security for the appearance of the accused, and bind over a person to appear and give evidence.

341.what: Section 341 states that any person who has been refused a complaint under section 340 or against whom such a complaint has been made may appeal to the superior court, which can direct the withdrawal of the complaint or make the complaint, and the order shall be final and not subject to revision.

342.what: Any Court dealing with an application made to it for filing a complaint under section 340 or an appeal under section 341, shall have power to make such order as to costs as may be just.

343.what: A Magistrate to whom a complaint is made under section 340 or section 341 shall, notwithstanding anything contained in Chapter XV, proceed, as far as may be, to deal with the case as if it were instituted on a police report. Where it is brought to the notice of such Magistrate, or of any other Magistrate to whom the case may have been transferred, that an appeal is pending against the decision arrived at in the judicial proceeding out of which the matter has arisen, he may, if he thinks fit, at any stage, adjourn the hearing of the case until such appeal is decided.

344.what: If a Court of Session or Magistrate of the first class expresses an opinion that any witness appeared in such proceeding had knowingly or wilfully given false evidence, it may take cognizance of the offence and try the offender summarily for giving or fabricating false evidence.

345.what: When an offence described in certain sections of the Indian Penal Code is committed in a court's view or presence, the court can detain the offender, take cognizance of the offence, sentence them to a fine not exceeding 200 rupees, and/or simple imprisonment for up to one month if the fine is not paid.

346.what: If the Court considers that a case should not be dealt with under section 345, it can forward the case to a Magistrate having jurisdiction to try the same and require security for the accused's appearance before the Magistrate.

347.what: A Registrar or Sub-Registrar is deemed a Civil Court when directed by the State Government under the Registration Act, 1908

348.what: A Court may discharge an offender or remit punishment on their submission to the order or requisition of such Court, or on apology being made to its satisfaction after being adjudged to punishment under section 345 or forwarded for trial under section 346.

349.what: If a witness refuses to answer questions or produce a document, the Court may sentence them to simple imprisonment for up to seven days if they do not offer a reasonable excuse after a reasonable opportunity has been given, unless they consent to be examined and answer or produce the document.

350.what: If any witness being summoned to appear before a Criminal Court is legally bound to appear at a certain place and time in obedience to the summons and without just excuse neglects or refuses to attend at that place or time or departs from the place where he has to attend before the time at which it is lawful for him to depart, and the Court before which the witness is to appear is satisfied that it is expedient in the interest of justice that such a witness should be tried summarily, the Court may take cognizance of the offence and after giving the offender an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be punished under this section, sentence him to fine not exceeding one hundred rupees.

351.what: A person sentenced in a court other than a High Court can appeal to the High Court, and certain provisions from Chapter XXIX apply.

352.what: No Judge of a Criminal Court (other than a Judge of a High Court) or Magistrate shall try any person for any offence referred to in section 195, when such offence is committed before himself or in contempt of his authority, or is brought under his notice as such Judge or Magistrate in the course of a judicial proceeding.

353.what: The judgment in every trial must be pronounced in open Court by the presiding officer immediately after the trial or at a later time with notice to the parties. The judgment can be delivered fully, read out fully, or explained with the operative part and its substance. The judgment must be dated and signed by the presiding officer.

354.what: Every judgment referred to in section 353 shall be written in the language of the Court; it shall contain the point or points for determination, the decision thereon and the reasons for the decision; it shall specify the offence (if any) of which, and the section of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) or other law under which, the accused is convicted, and the punishment to which he is sentenced; if it be a judgment of acquittal, shall state the offence of which the accused is acquitted and direct that he be set at liberty.

355.what: A Metropolitan Magistrate must record specific details when making a judgment, including: case number, date of offence commission, complainant's name, accused person's name and residence, nature of offence, accused's plea and examination, final order date, and reasons for decision in appeal cases.

356.what: This section states that when a previously convicted offender is again convicted of an offence punishable under certain sections of the Indian Penal Code with imprisonment for three years or upwards, the court may order that their residence and any change of or absence from it after release be notified for a term not exceeding five years.

357.what: Section 357 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the following rules: When a Court imposes a sentence of fine or a sentence (including a sentence of death) of which fine forms a part, the Court may order the whole or any part of the fine to be applied in defraying expenses incurred in prosecution, paying compensation for loss or injury caused by the offence, compensating persons entitled to damages under Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, or compensating bona fide purchasers of stolen property. However, the fine cannot be paid before an appeal has been presented or decided. Additionally, if the person against whom an offence has been committed belongs to Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes, the Court may order the whole or any part of the fine recovered to be applied when passing judgment, except in cases where both parties belong to the same group.

357A.what: Every State Government in co-ordination with the Central Government shall prepare a scheme for providing funds for the purpose of compensation to the victim or his dependents who have suffered loss or injury as a result of the crime and who require rehabilitation.

357B.what: The compensation payable by the State Government under section 357A shall be in addition to the payment of fine to the victim.

357C.what: All hospitals, public or private, whether run by the Central Government, the State Government, local bodies or any other person, shall immediately provide the first-aid or medical treatment, free of cost, to the victims of any offence covered under section 326A, 376, 4[376A, 376AB, 376B, 376C, 376D , 376DA, 376DB] or section 376E of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), and shall immediately inform the police of such incident.

358.what: A Magistrate can award compensation of up to ₹1,000 to a person who was groundlessly arrested, including the loss of time and expenses. If multiple people were arrested, each may receive compensation. The amount cannot be recovered as a fine; instead, the person liable must pay or face up to 30 days in simple imprisonment.

359.what: The court may order the accused to pay costs incurred by the complainant in addition to the penalty imposed, and may impose simple imprisonment for up to 30 days if payment is not made.

360.what: Section 360 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the conditions for releasing an offender on probation. According to this section, a person convicted of an offence punishable with fine only or with imprisonment for a term of seven years or less, or a minor/first offender convicted of an offence not punishable with death or imprisonment for life, may be released on probation of good conduct if the Court considers it expedient. The release is conditional on the offender entering into a bond to appear and receive sentence when called upon during a period not exceeding three years. Additionally, the offender must have a fixed place of abode or regular occupation in the area where the court acts, and be likely to live there during the period of their probation.

361.what: Where in any case the Court could have dealt with an accused person under section 360 or under the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 (20 of 1958); or a youthful offender under the Children Act, 1960 (60 of 1960) or any other law for the time being in force for the treatment, training or rehabilitation of youthful offenders, but has not done so, it shall record in its judgment the special reasons for not having done so.

362.what: Save as otherwise provided by this Code or by any other law for the time being in force, no Court, when it has signed its judgment or final order disposing of a case, shall alter or review the same except to correct a clerical or arithmetical error.

363.what: This section states that when an accused is sentenced to imprisonment, a copy of the judgment must be given to them free of cost immediately after pronouncement. Additionally, if they apply for a certified copy or translation, it will be provided without delay and free of cost in cases where the judgment can be appealed by the accused.

364.what: The original judgment must be filed with the court record. If the original judgment is in a language other than the court's language, it must be translated into the court's language and added to the record if the accused requests it.

365.what: The Court of Session must send a copy of its finding and sentence to the District Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the trial was held, if the case is tried by the Court or a Chief Judicial Magistrate.

366.what: When the Court of Session passes a sentence of death, the proceedings shall be submitted to the High Court for confirmation, and the sentence will not be executed until it is confirmed by the High Court.

367.what: The High Court may make further inquiry into a point bearing upon the guilt or innocence of the convicted person, take additional evidence, or direct it to be made or taken by the Court of Session.

368.what: The High Court can confirm a sentence, pass another sentence, annul a conviction, convict the accused of another offence, order a new trial, or acquit the accused, subject to certain conditions and time limits.

369.what: In every case so submitted, the confirmation of the sentence, or any new sentence or order passed by the High Court, shall, when such Court consists of two or more Judges, be made, passed and signed by at least two of them.

370.what: Where any such case is heard before a Bench of Judges and such Judges are equally divided in opinion, the case shall be decided in the manner provided by section 392.

371.what: In cases submitted by the Court of Session to the High Court for the confirmation of a sentence of death, the proper officer of the High Court shall, without delay, after the order of confirmation or other order has been made by the High Court, send a copy of the order, under the seal of the High Court and attested with his official signature, to the Court of Session.

372.what: No appeal can be filed from a Criminal Court's judgment or order unless specified in this Code or other laws, except for specific cases where the victim has the right to appeal against acquittal, conviction for a lesser offence, or inadequate compensation.

373.what: Any person who has been ordered under section 117 to give security for keeping the peace or for good behaviour, or who is aggrieved by any order refusing to accept or rejecting a surety under section 121, may appeal against such order to the Court of Session.

374.what:
A person convicted in certain cases can appeal to specific courts: 
 A person convicted by a High Court can appeal to the Supreme Court.
 A person convicted by a Sessions Judge or other court with a sentence of over 7 years can appeal to the High Court.
 A person convicted by a Metropolitan Magistrate or Assistant Sessions Judge can appeal to the Court of Session, unless they were sentenced under section 325 or had an order/sentence made/passed under section 360.

375.what: Section 375 states that there shall be no appeal by a convicted person in certain cases where the conviction is by a High Court or a Court of Session, Metropolitan Magistrate or Magistrate of the first or second class, except as to the extent or legality of the sentence.

376.what: A convicted person cannot appeal in cases where a sentence is: imprisonment for 6 months or less and/or a fine of ₹1000 or less; imprisonment for 3 months or less and/or a fine of ₹200 or less; a fine of ₹100 or less; or a fine of ₹200 or less in a summary case, unless another punishment is combined with the fine.

377.what: The State Government may direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy to the Court of Session or High Court, depending on the court that passed the sentence.

378.what: The District Magistrate may direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal to the Court of 1. Subs. by Act 25 of 2005, s. 31, for certain words (w.e.f. 23-6-2006). 2.
