(6) If, in any case, the application under sub-section ( 4) for the grant of special leave to appeal from an order of acquittal is refused, no appeal from that order of acquittal shall lie under sub-section ( 1) or under sub-section (2).

379.what: The High Court can be appealed to by the accused if they were previously acquitted but then found guilty again by the High Court and sentenced to death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years in prison.

380.what: Notwithstanding anything contained in this Chapter, when more persons than one are convicted in one trial, and an appealable judgment or order has been passed in respect of any of such persons, all or any of the persons convicted at such trial shall have a right of appeal.

381.what: (1) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), an appeal to the Court of Session or Sessions Judge shall be heard by the Sessions Judge or by an Additional Sessions Judge: Provided that an appeal against a conviction on a trial held by a Magistrate of the second class may be heard and disposed of by an Assistant Sessions Judge or a Chief Judicial Magistrate. (2) An Additional Sessions Judge, Assistant Sessions Judge or a Chief Judicial Magistrate shall hear only such appeals as the Sessions Judge of the division may, by general or special order, make over to him or as the High Court may, by special order, direct him to hear.

382.what: Every appeal shall be made in the form of a petition in writing presented by the appellant or his pleader, and every such petition shall (unless the Court to which it is presented otherwise directs) be accompanied by a copy of the judgment or order appealed against.

383.what: If you are in jail, you can give your appeal petition and copies to the jail officer, who will send them to the correct court.

384.what: The Appellate Court may dismiss an appeal summarily if it considers that there is no sufficient ground for interfering, but only after giving the appellant a reasonable opportunity to be heard, unless the appeal is frivolous or the accused's presence would cause inconvenience disproportionate to the case.

385.what: If an Appellate Court does not dismiss an appeal summarily, it must give notice to the following people: the appellant or their pleader, a government-appointed officer, the complainant (if the appeal is from a complaint case), and the accused (if the appeal is under sections 377 or 378). The court must also provide a copy of the grounds for appeal. If the appeal is only about sentence severity, the court may decide without hearing the record.

386.what: The Appellate Court may dismiss the appeal, reverse such order and direct that further inquiry be made, or that the accused be re-tried or committed for trial, as the case may be, or find him guilty and pass sentence on him according to law.

387.what: The rules contained in Chapter XXVII as to the judgment of a Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall apply, so far as may be practicable, to the judgment in appeal of a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate: Provided that, unless the Appellate Court otherwise directs, the accused shall not be brought up, or required to attend, to hear judgment delivered.

388.what: The High Court must certify its judgment or order to the lower court that decided the appeal, and if the lower court is a Judicial Magistrate other than the Chief Judicial Magistrate, the High Court's judgment or order shall be sent through the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and if it is an Executive Magistrate, the District Magistrate.

389.what: The Appellate Court may suspend the execution of a sentence pending appeal and release the convicted person on bail or their own bond, but only after giving the Public Prosecutor an opportunity to show cause in writing.

390.what: The taking of evidence under this section shall be subject to the provisions of Chapter XXIII, as if it were an inquiry.

391.what: The Appellate Court may take further evidence or direct it to be taken by a Magistrate or, when the Appellate Court is a High Court, by a Court of Session or a Magistrate, and the accused or his pleader shall have the right to be present when the additional evidence is taken.

392.what: When an appeal under this Chapter is heard by a High Court before a Bench of Judges and they are divided in opinion, the appeal, with their opinions, shall be laid before another Judge of that Court, and that Judge, after such hearing as he thinks fit, shall deliver his opinion, and the judgment or order shall follow that opinion: Provided that if one of the Judges constituting the Bench, or, where the appeal is laid before another Judge under this section, that Judge, so requires, the appeal shall be re-heard and decided by a larger Bench of Judges.

393.what: Judgments and orders passed by an Appellate Court are final, except in cases where an appeal is made against conviction, acquittal, or sentence enhancement, as specified in other sections.

394.what: Every other appeal under section 377 or section 378 shall finally abate on the death of the accused. Every other appeal under this Chapter (except an appeal from a sentence of fine) shall finally abate on the death of the appellant: Provided that where the appeal is against a conviction and sentence of death or of imprisonment, and the appellant dies during the pendency of the appeal, any of his near relatives may, within thirty days of the death of the appellant, apply to the Appellate Court for leave to continue the appeal; and if leave is granted, the appeal shall not abate.

395.what: A court can refer a case involving a question about the validity of an Act, Ordinance, Regulation, or provision to the High Court if it is not already decided by the High Court or Supreme Court.

396.what: The High Court shall pass such order thereon as it thinks fit, and shall cause a copy of such order to be sent to the Court by which the reference was made, which shall dispose of the case conformably to the said order.

397.what: The High Court or Sessions Judge can call for and examine records from inferior Criminal Courts to check if findings, sentences, or orders are correct, legal, or proper. They can also suspend sentence execution and release an accused on bail or bond while the record is examined.

398.what: The High Court or the Sessions Judge may direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate to make further inquiry into a complaint that has been dismissed under section 203 or sub-section (4) of section 204, or into the case of any person accused of an offence who has been discharged.

399.what: The Sessions Judge can exercise all powers of the High Court in certain cases, including reviewing decisions made by lower courts. The decision of the Sessions Judge on a revision application is final and cannot be appealed to the High Court or another court.

400.what: An Additional Sessions Judge shall have and may exercise all the powers of a Sessions Judge under this Chapter in respect of any case which may be transferred to him by or under any general or special order of the Sessions Judge.

401.what: The High Court may, in its discretion, exercise any of the powers conferred on a Court of Appeal by sections 386, 389, 390 and 391 or on a Court of Session by section 307, and when the Judges composing the Court of Revision are equally divided in opinion, the case shall be disposed of in the manner provided by section 392.

402.what: The High Court has the power to withdraw or transfer revision cases, and it shall decide which court should finally dispose of the applications for revision, taking into account the general convenience of the parties and the importance of the questions involved.

403.what: No party has a right to be heard personally or by pleader before any Court exercising its powers of revision, but the Court may hear any party if it thinks fit.

404.what: When the record of any trial held by a Metropolitan Magistrate is called for by the High Court or Court of Session under section 397, the Magistrate may submit with the record a statement setting forth the grounds of his decision or order and any facts which he thinks material to the issue, and that Court shall consider such statement before overruling or setting aside the said decision or order.

405.what: When a case is revised under this Chapter by the High Court or a Sessions Judge, it or he shall, in the manner provided by section 388, certify its decision or order to the Court by which the finding, sentence or order revised was recorded or passed, and the Court to which the decision or order is so certified shall thereupon make such orders as are conformable to the decision so certified, and, if necessary, the record shall be amended in accordance therewith.

406.what: The Supreme Court may transfer cases and appeals between High Courts or Criminal Courts of equal or superior jurisdiction, on the application of the Attorney-General of India or a party interested, with certain conditions.

407.what: The High Court may transfer cases and appeals from subordinate courts to itself or other courts of equal or superior jurisdiction, subject to certain conditions and procedures.

408.what: The Sessions Judge has the power to transfer cases and appeals from one Criminal Court to another Criminal Court in his sessions division, provided that an order under this sub-section is expedient for the ends of justice.

409.what: A Sessions Judge may withdraw any case or appeal from, or recall any case or appeal which he has made over to, any Assistant Sessions Judge or Chief Judicial Magistrate subordinate to him.

410.what: Any Chief Judicial Magistrate may withdraw any case from, or recall any case which he has made over to, any Magistrate subordinate to him, and may inquire into or try such case himself, or refer it for inquiry or trial to any other such Magistrate competent to inquire into or try the same.

411.what: A District Magistrate or Sub- Divisional Magistrate can transfer a started case to a lower magistrate, withdraw a case from the higher magistrate, or decide on it themselves.

412.what: A Sessions Judge or Magistrate must explain why they made an order under certain sections.

413.what: When in a case submitted to the High Court for the confirmation of a sentence of death, the Court of Session receives the order of confirmation or other order of the High Court thereon, it shall cause such order to be carried into effect by issuing a warrant or taking such other steps as may be necessary.

414.what: The Court of Session shall, on receiving the order of the High Court, cause the sentence to be carried into effect by issuing a warrant.

415.what: A person sentenced to death by a High Court can have their execution postponed if they appeal to the Supreme Court. The postponement will continue until the appeal is disposed of or the time limit for appealing has expired.

416.what: If a woman sentenced to death is found to be pregnant, the High Court shall commute the sentence to imprisonment for life.

417.what: The State Government may direct in what place any person liable to be imprisoned or committed to custody under this Code shall be confined, and if any person is in confinement in a civil jail, the Court or Magistrate ordering the imprisonment or committal may direct that the person be removed to a criminal jail.

418.what: The court passing the sentence shall forthwith forward a warrant to the jail or other place in which the accused is, or is to be, confined, and, unless the accused is already confined in such jail or other place, shall forward him to such jail or other place, with the warrant.

419.what: Every warrant for the execution of a sentence of imprisonment must be directed to the officer in charge of the jail where the prisoner is being held.

420.what: The warrant for a prisoner's confinement must be lodged with the jailor.

421.what: The Court passing the sentence may take action for the recovery of the fine in either or both of the following ways, that is to say, it may— (a) issue a warrant for the levy of the amount by attachment and sale of any movable property belonging to the offender; (b) issue a warrant to the Collector of the district, authorising him to realise the amount as arrears of land revenue from the movable or immovable property, or both, of the defaulter

422.what: A warrant issued under clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 421 by any Court may be executed within the local jurisdiction of such Court, and it shall authorise the attachment and sale of any such property outside such jurisdiction, when it is endorsed by the District Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction such property is found.

423.what: Notwithstanding anything contained in this Code or in any other law for the time being in force, when an offender has been sentenced to pay a fine by a Criminal Court in any territory to which this Code does not extend and the Court passing the sentence issues a warrant to the Collector of a district in the territories to which this Code extends, authorising him to realise the amount as if it were an arrear of land revenue, such warrant shall be deemed to be a warrant issued under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 421 by a Court in the territories to which this Code extends, and the provisions of sub-section (3) of the said section as to the execution of such warrant shall apply accordingly.

424.what: This section states that when an offender has been sentenced to fine only and to imprisonment in default of payment of the fine, the court may order the fine to be payable in full on a certain date or in instalments, suspend the execution of the sentence of imprisonment and release the offender on condition of appearing before the court, and direct the sentence of imprisonment to be carried into execution if the fine is not paid.

425.what: A warrant can be issued by a judge or magistrate who originally sentenced someone, or their replacement.

426.what: When a sentence of death, imprisonment for life or fine is passed under this Code on an escaped convict, such sentence shall take effect immediately. If the sentence is not severer in kind than the sentence being served, it takes effect after serving the remaining time of the original sentence.

427.what: When a person already serving an imprisonment sentence will start serving a new sentence at the end of their current one unless the court decides otherwise. If someone is sentenced to a longer prison term while already serving a shorter one, they can serve both sentences at the same time.

428.what: The period of detention undergone by an accused person before conviction can be set off against their imprisonment sentence.

429.what: Nothing in section 426 or section 427 shall be held to excuse any person from any part of the punishment to which he is liable upon his former or subsequent conviction. (2) When an award of imprisonment in default of payment of a fine is annexed to a substantive sentence of imprisonment and the person undergoing the sentence is after its execution to undergo a further substantive sentence or further substantive sentences of imprisonment, effect shall not be given to the award of imprisonment in default of payment of the fine until the person has undergone the further sentence or sentences.

430.what: When a sentence has been fully executed, the officer executing it shall return the warrant to the Court from which it is issued, with an endorsement under his hand certifying the manner in which the sentence has been executed.

431.what: Any money (other than a fine) payable by virtue of any order made under this Code, and the method of recovery of which is not otherwise expressly provided for, shall be recoverable as if it were a fine: Provided that section 421 shall, in its application to an order under section 359, by virtue of this section, be construed as if in the proviso to sub-section ( 1) of section 421, after the words and figures “under section 357”, the words and figures “or an order for payment of costs under section 359” had been inserted.

432.what: The appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence or remit the whole or any part of the punishment to which a person has been sentenced without conditions or upon conditions accepted by the person sentenced.

433.what: The appropriate Government may commute a sentence without the person's consent, except in certain cases: death can be replaced with another punishment, life imprisonment can be replaced with up to 14 years or a fine, rigorous imprisonment can be replaced with simple imprisonment or a fine, and simple imprisonment can be replaced with a fine.

433A.what: A person serving a life sentence cannot be released from prison until they have served at least 14 years.

434.what: The powers conferred by sections 432 and 433 upon the State Government may, in the case of sentences of death, also be exercised by the Central Government.

435.what: The State Government can only exercise its power to remit or commute a sentence in cases where the sentence is for an offence investigated by the Delhi Special Police Establishment or any other agency empowered to make investigation into an offence under a Central Act, and the offence involves misappropriation or destruction of property belonging to the Central Government, or was committed by a person in the service of the Central Government while acting in his official duty.

436.what: A person arrested or detained without warrant can give bail and be released if they are not accused of a non-bailable offence, and if they can afford surety. If they cannot afford surety, they may be discharged on executing a bond without sureties.

436A.what: Section 436A states that an undertrial prisoner can be detained for a maximum period of one-half of the maximum imprisonment specified for the offence, and must be released on personal bond or bail if detention is longer than this period.

437.what: Section 437 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the conditions under which a person accused of a non-bailable offence can be released on bail. According to this section, a person accused of a non-bailable offence can be released on bail if they are arrested without warrant, appear in court, or are suspected of committing the offence. However, this is not allowed if the offence is punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or if the accused has been previously convicted of such an offence.The court may direct release on bail if the accused is under 16 years old, a woman, sick, or infirm. The court can also consider releasing the accused on bail if it's just and proper to do so for any other special reason.Additionally, the court must give an opportunity to the Public Prosecutor before releasing the accused on bail if the offence is punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or seven years or more.A person accused of a non-bailable offence must be released on bail after 60 days from the first date fixed for taking evidence, unless the Magistrate records reasons in writing for not releasing them. Furthermore, a court may direct a person released on bail to be arrested and committed to custody if necessary. This section ensures that the rights of both the accused and the state are balanced, allowing for the release of the accused on bail while also ensuring that justice is served.

437A.what: Before conclusion of the trial and before disposal of the appeal, the Court trying the offence or the Appellate Court, as the case may be, shall require the accused to execute bail bonds with sureties, to appear before the higher Court as and when such Court issues notice in respect of any appeal or petition filed against the judgment of the respective Court and such bail bonds shall be in force for six months.

438.what: Section 438 of The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 explains the procedure for granting bail to a person accused of committing a non-bailable offence. According to this section, a person who believes they may be arrested on accusation of committing such an offence can apply to the High Court or Court of Session for direction under this section. If the court thinks fit, it can direct that in case of arrest, the person shall be released on bail. The conditions for bail include: making self available for interrogation, not dissuading anyone from disclosing facts, not leaving India without permission, and other conditions as imposed by the court. Additionally, a person who is apprehended of arrest can request a court for bail release, and if granted, they will be subject to the provisions of section 437.

439.what: A High Court or Court of Session may direct that any person accused of an offence and in custody be released on bail, and if the offence is of the nature specified in sub-section (3) of section 437, may impose any condition which it considers necessary for the purposes mentioned in that sub-section.

440.what: The amount of every bond executed under this Chapter shall be fixed with due regard to the circumstances of the case and shall not be excessive. The High Court or the Court of Session may direct that the bail required by a police officer or Magistrate be reduced.

441.what: Section 441 states that before a person is released on bail or on their own bond, they must execute a bond with a sufficient sum of money, and when released on bail, they must attend at the specified time and place until otherwise directed by the police officer or Court.

441A.what: Every person standing surety to an accused person must declare in court how many people they have stood surety for, including the accused, and provide all necessary details.

442.what: This section states that as soon as the bond has been executed, the person for whose appearance it has been executed shall be released. If the person is in jail, the court admitting them to bail shall issue an order of release to the officer in charge of the jail, who shall then release them.

443.what: This section states that if insufficient sureties have been accepted or become insufficient, the Court may issue a warrant of arrest and order the person released on bail to find sufficient sureties. If they fail to do so, the person may be committed to jail.

444.what: Section 444 states that a person released on bail may apply to discharge the bond at any time, and if the Magistrate is satisfied with the reason for discharge, he shall issue a warrant of arrest directing the person to appear before him.

445.what: A court or officer may allow a person to deposit money instead of executing a bond with sureties, except for bonds related to good behavior.

446.what: Section 446 states that when a bond under this Code is forfeited, the court shall record the grounds of proof and may call upon any person bound by such bond to pay the penalty or show cause why it should not be paid.

446A.what: Cancellation of bond and bail bond: If a person's bond is forfeited due to breach of condition, their existing bond (and any bonds by sureties) are cancelled. They can only be released if the Police Officer or Court believes there was no sufficient reason for not meeting the bond conditions. They may be released on a new bond if the authorities think it's sufficient.

447.what: The Court by whose order such bond was taken, or a Magistrate of the first class may order the person from whom such security was demanded to furnish fresh securities in accordance with the directions of the original order, and if such security is not furnished, such Court or Magistrate may proceed as if there had been a default in complying with such original order.

448.what: When the person required by any Court, or officer to execute a bond is a minor, such Court or officer may accept, in lieu thereof, a bond executed by a surety or sureties only.

449.what: All orders passed under section 446 shall be appealable,— (i) in the case of an order made by a Magistrate, to the Sessions Judge; (ii) in the case of an order made by a Court of Session, to the Court to which an appeal lies from an order made by such Court.

450.what: The High Court or Court of Sessions may direct any Magistrate to levy the amount due on a bond for appearance or attendance at such High Court.

451.what: This section states that when any property is produced before a Criminal Court during an inquiry or trial, the Court may make an order for its proper custody pending the conclusion of the inquiry or trial. The Court can also order the sale or disposal of the property if it is subject to speedy and natural decay or if it is expedient to do so.

452.what: This section outlines the procedures for the disposal of property at the conclusion of a trial, including destruction, confiscation, delivery to a person claiming possession, or other means. The Court can also direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate to deal with the property in certain cases.

453.what: When any person is convicted of any offence which includes, or amounts to, theft or receiving stolen property, and it is proved that any other person bought the stolen property from him without knowing or having reason to believe that the same was stolen, and that any money has on his arrest been taken out of the possession of the convicted person, the Court may, on the application of such purchaser and on the restitution of the stolen property to the person entitled to the possession thereof, order that out of such money a sum not exceeding the price paid by such purchaser be delivered to him.

454.what: A person can appeal against an order made under sections 452 or 453 to the court that normally handles appeals from convictions by the original court.

455.what: The Court may order the destruction of all copies of libellous and other matter in respect of which the conviction was had, and which are in the custody of the Court or remain in the possession or power of the person convicted.

456.what: When a person is convicted of an offence attended by criminal force or show of force or by criminal intimidation, the Court may order that possession of immovable property be restored to that person after evicting any other person who may be in possession of the property.

457.what: The Magistrate may make an order regarding the disposal of seized property, delivery to the rightful owner, or custody and production if the owner cannot be ascertained.

458.what: If no person establishes their claim to property within 6 months, and the owner cannot prove it was legally acquired, the Magistrate can direct the State Government to sell the property. The sale proceeds will be handled according to prescribed rules.

459.what: The Magistrate may direct the sale of perishable property if it is unknown or absent and its value is less than five hundred rupees, or if the Magistrate believes that selling the property would be for the benefit of the owner.

460.what: If a Magistrate who is not authorized to perform certain tasks performs them in good faith, their proceedings will not be invalidated.

461.what: If any Magistrate, not being empowered by law in this behalf, does any of the following things, namely:— (a) attaches and sells property under section 83; (b) issues a search-warrant for a document, parcel or other things in the custody of a postal or telegraph authority; (c) demands security to keep the peace; (d) demands security for good behaviour; (e) discharges a person lawfully bound to be of good behaviour; (f) cancels a bond to keep the peace; (g) makes an order for maintenance; (h) makes an order under section 133 as to a local nuisance; (i) prohibits, under section 143, the repetition or continuance of a public nuisance; (j) makes an order under Part C or Part D of Chapter X; (k) takes cognizance of an offence under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 190; (l) tries an offender; (m) tries an offender summarily; (n) passes a sentence, under section 325, on proceedings recorded by another Magistrate; (o) decides an appeal; (p) calls, under section 397, for proceedings; or (q) revises an order passed under section 446, his proceedings shall be void.

462.what: A Criminal Court's finding, sentence, or order cannot be overturned because the proceedings took place in the wrong location, unless this mistake caused a miscarriage of justice.

463.what: If any Court before which a confession or other statement of an accused person recorded, or purporting to be recorded under section 164 or section 281, is tendered, or has been received, in evidence finds that any of the provisions of either of such sections have not been complied with by the Magistrate recording the statement, it may take evidence in regard to such non-compliance and admit such statement if satisfied that such non-compliance has not injured the accused in his defence on the merits and that he duly made the statement recorded.

464.what: If a court makes a mistake with the charges, and this mistake causes unfairness to the defendant, the court can fix the mistake. If the mistake caused unfairness, the court may order a new trial or quash (cancel) the conviction if it's not fair to charge the defendant with the facts proven.

465.what: No finding, sentence or order passed by a Court of competent jurisdiction shall be reversed or altered by a Court of appeal, confirmation of revision on account of any error, omission or irregularity in the complaint, summons, warrant, proclamation, order, judgment or other proceedings before or during trial or in any inquiry or other proceedings under this Code, or any error, or irregularity in any sanction for the prosecution, unless in the opinion of that Court, a failure of justice has in fact been occasioned thereby.

466.what: No attachment made under this Code shall be deemed unlawful due to defects or errors in summonses, convictions, writs of attachment, or other related proceedings.

467.what: For the purposes of this Chapter, unless the context otherwise requires, “period of limitation” means the period specified in section 468 for taking cognizance of an offence.

468.what: No Court can take cognizance of an offence after its limitation period expires, except in certain cases.

469.what: The period of limitation in relation to an offender shall commence on the date of the offence, or where the commission of the offence was not known to the person aggrieved by the offence or to any police officer, the first day on which such offence comes to the knowledge of such person or to any police officer, whichever is earlier; or where it is not known by whom the offence was committed, the first day on which the identity of the offender is known to the person aggrieved by the offence or to the police officer making investigation into the offence, whichever is earlier.

470.what: The period of limitation for a crime does not include time spent: - Prosecuting another case against the same person in good faith. - Waiting for an injunction to expire. - Getting permission from the government or other authorities. - Being outside India or avoiding arrest.

471.what: A Court shall be deemed to be closed on any day within the meaning of this section, if, during its normal working hours, it remains closed on that day.

472.what: In the case of a continuing offence, a fresh period of limitation shall begin to run at every moment of the time during which the offence continues.

473.what: Any court may take cognizance of an offence after the expiry of the period of limitation, if it is satisfied on the facts and in the circumstances of the case that the delay has been properly explained or that it is necessary so to do in the interests of justice.

474.what: When an offence is tried by the High Court, it must follow the same procedures as a Court of Sessions would if it were trying that case.

475.what: The Central Government may make rules consistent with this Code and other laws relating to the Armed Forces of the Union, for cases in which persons subject to military law are tried by a Court to which this Code applies or by a Court-martial; Magistrates shall deliver accused persons to commanding officers for trial by a Court-martial.

476.what: Forms can be used with variations to suit individual cases, and using them is considered sufficient.

477.what: Every High Court may make rules with the previous approval of the State Government, regulating matters such as petition-writers in Criminal Courts, licences, business conduct, and fees.

478.what: The State Government may direct that references to an Executive Magistrate shall be construed as references to a Judicial Magistrate of the first class after consulting with the High Court and obtaining permission from the Legislative Assembly.

479.what: No Judge or Magistrate shall, except with the permission of the Court to which an appeal lies from his Court, try or commit for trial any case to or in which he is a party, or personally interested, and no Judge or Magistrate shall hear an appeal from any judgment or order passed or made by himself.

480.what: No pleader who practises in the Court of any Magistrate shall sit as a Magistrate in that Court or in any Court within the local jurisdiction of that Court.

481.what: A public servant having any duty to perform in connection with the sale of any property under this Code shall not purchase or bid for the property.

482.what: Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

483.what: Every High Court shall so exercise its superintendence over the Courts of Judicial Magistrates subordinate to it as to ensure that there is an expeditious and proper disposal of cases by such Magistrates.

484.what: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (5 of 1898), is hereby repealed. Notwithstanding such repeal— (a) if, immediately before the date on which this Code comes into force, there is any appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation pending, then, such appeal, application, trial, inquiry or investigation shall be disposed of, continued, held or made, as the case may be, in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (5 of 1898), as in force immediately before such commencement (hereinafter referred to as the old Code), as if this Code had not come into force: Provided that every inquiry under Chapter XVIII of the Old Code, which is pending at the commencement of this Code, shall be dealt with and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of this Code; (b) all notifications published, proclamations issued, powers conferred, forms prescribed, local jurisdictions defined, sentences passed and orders, rules and appointments, not being appointments as Special Magistrates, made under the Old Code and which are in force immediately before the commencement of this Code, shall be deemed, respectively, to have been published, issued, conferred, prescribed, defined, passed or made under the corresponding provisions of this Code; (c) any sanction accorded or consent given under the Old Code in pursuance of which no proceeding was commenced under that Code, shall be deemed to have been accorded or given under the corresponding provisions of this Code and proceedings may be commenced under this Code in pursuance of such sanction of consent; (d) the provisions of the Old Code shall continue to apply in relation to every prosecution against a Ruler within the meaning of article 363 of the Constitution.
